Jin caught the dull glint of carbon-fiber boarding ladders slung across their thwarts and pneumatic grappling guns resting on their bows. No blue flags. No sovereign coast guard insignia. Apex Marine Tactical.

They were not here to serve paperwork. They were here to disable the node’s independent power before dawn.

"Aisyah! Are the intake lines clear?" Jin barked, reaching the pump manifold beneath the crane's forward pylon.

"Silt filter’s half-choked from the tide change!" her voice crackled over the hardwired speaker near the valve cluster. "I’ve got the bypass open, but the salt crust is jamming the secondary gate!"

"Take the sledge to the bypass ring!" Rui grunted, throwing his full weight against a three-foot bronze spanner on the sea-cock valve. The bilateral strain in his forearms made his sinews tremble violently, his skin slick with sweat and brine. "Move! They’re inside two hundred yards!"

The lead interceptor throttled up. The low rumble became an aggressive, throaty snarl as its twin props bit into the shallow basin. A narrow, high-intensity spotlight punched out from its console, spearing across the rusted hull of the slipway, hunting for the main electrical umbilical connecting the tidal turbine bank to the shore manifold.

The beam struck Jin full in the chest. 

*Crack.* 

A pneumatic grapple arched upward through the squall, its four-pronged titanium hook clattering violently over the lower catwalk railing of Berth 9. The heavy Kevlar climbing line snapped taut against the pier edge as the lead skiff reversed thrusters to hold station against the stone quay.

"Rui! Turn it!" Jin yelled.

With a ragged cry, Rui slammed the bronze wheel past its corroded stop. Inside the cast-iron housing beneath their feet, four hundred gallons of pressurized seawater hit the line with a shudder that jarred Jin’s teeth. 

Jin lunged for the dual-grip tiller of the primary salvage monitor mounted to the dock edge—a heavy brass cannon salvaged from an ocean-going firefighting tug, its swivel joint stiff with aged tallow. He dropped his shoulder into the counterweight, dragging the nozzle downward until the sights lined with the black rubber sponson of the lead boat.

"Brace!" Jin bellowed.

He threw the quarter-turn lever.

The sea roared back through the pipe. A solid column of green ocean water, six inches thick and pressurized to bursting, erupted from the nozzle. The recoil slammed into Jin’s chest like an iron slab, driving the heels of his boots back two inches into the rain-slick planks.

The jet struck the water three yards short of the lead interceptor, throwing up an blinding wall of spray that completely swallowed the boat’s spotlight. Jin adjusted his footing, driving his hips forward, and elevated the iron barrel.

The high-pressure torrent slammed directly into the skiff’s bow. 

Under the crushing kinetic impact of twelve tons of moving water per minute, the light composite craft didn't just swerve—its bow was forced violently down into the chop. The boarding ladder shattered like dry bamboo. Two mercenaries on the foredeck were swept clean off their feet, thrown across the center console into the engine well by the sheer hydraulic mass.

The gunboat’s engine shrieked as its propellers broke surface, churning air, before the boat slid sideways, taking hundreds of gallons over its port gunwale.

"Second boat on the jetty flank!" Lin’s voice echoed down from the crane gantry over the sound-powered telephone horn. "They're attempting a cut on the sub-surface cable!"

Jin swung the monitor. The brass collar groaned, protesting the lateral torque. The jet carved a boiling trench across the basin water, slicing through the midnight drizzle until it caught the second craft broadside. 

The jet sheared off the skiff’s outboard cowling with a metallic crunch, crushing the composite shroud into the cooling fan. White steam erupted as salt water flooded the hot cylinder block. The craft lurched violently, dead in the water, wallowing heavily as its self-bailing scuppers choked on river debris.

From the deck of the third skiff, twenty yards back, an operative raised a compressed-gas launcher. A blinding canister arced through the dark, striking the gantry crane’s iron stanchion and bursting into a dense, chemical aerosol curtain of gray tear gas.

The wind from the sea caught the cloud, rolling it directly into the pump bay.

Jin pulled his collar over his mouth, coughing violently. His lungs burned, the old bunker-fuel damage flaring into an agonized spasm that forced him to his knees. Rui fell beside him, retching onto the iron grating, his eyes streaming with tears.

"Aisyah..." Jin wheezed, his vision blurring.

Above them, the high-pitched whine of the gantry’s auxiliary hoist screeched into life.

Aisyah hadn't abandoned the crane controls. From her perch forty feet above the waterline, she threw the manual brake on the gantry’s empty spreader bar. 

Six tons of structural steel dropped straight down through the darkness.

It did not hit the skiff; it plummeted into the water four feet off its starboard beam. The displaced tidal surge slammed against the third craft with the force of a rogue wave, flipping the light interceptor onto its beam ends. The crew was hurled into the churning, oily blackness of the slipway basin.

The surviving first boat, half-swamped and its console smashed by water pressure, scrambled to engage its bow thrusters, desperately hauling its sodden comrades out of the chop. Its searchlight was dead, its electronics ruined by the sheer volume of salt brine that had drowned its open cockpits. 

Without firing a single shot, the remaining tactical craft backed frantically into the fairway, trailing oily foam and severed lines, its sirens dead, its crew shivering and defeated by the pure, unyielding mass of the sea.

Silence fell over Berth 9, broken only by the hiss of the receding wake against the stone wall and the ragged, gasping breaths of the three people on the valve platform.

Rui sat with his head between his knees, spitting clear saliva, his forearms trembling uncontrollably. Lin appeared at the bottom of the ladder, carrying a lantern shielded with a piece of cardboard, her face smudged with soot.

"They're clearing the channel," she whispered, her voice shaking. "They won't try the basin again tonight."

Jin pulled himself upright by the monitor's brass handle. His uniform was soaked through, cold mud caked across his shins. He looked down at the dark water where the skiffs had retreated.

Something bobbed against the wooden fender piles.

It was not a man, and it was not a shattered spar. It was a heavy, waterproof flight case that had been thrown from the swamped command boat, caught in the eddy behind the jetty.

Rui leaned over the edge with a boat hook, dragging the dripping plastic case onto the dock. The latches were sealed with red customs tape.

Jin dropped to one knee and thumbed the release.

Inside, resting on die-cut foam, was a commercial satellite terminal wired to a ruggedized field tablet. The screen was still illuminated under its tempered glass, displaying an active admiralty recovery ledger that updated every three seconds.

At the top of the queue, glowing amber in the darkness, was the registration of the Keppel-Batam shipyard itself.

Beneath it was the order authorization timestamped forty minutes ago, signed by the same hijacked credential. But beneath Jin’s forged name, a new field had populated, linking the Batam receiver’s terminal to an offshore operating account in Singapore.

The name on the beneficiary line made Jin’s breath catch in his throat.

It was not Euro-Asian Maritime Finance. 

It was the personal pension trust of Captain Jin Wei's own missing chief engineer—the one man who had gone down with the *Bintang Laut* three years ago.

label: Chapter 8
title: The First Founders' Covenant Assembly on the deck of a dry-docked freighter under the 5-Minute rule
content:
The name on the beneficiary line burned into the damp glass of the screen: *Harun bin Idris*. 

Captain Jin Wei did not blink. The salt crust around his eyelashes pulled tight, a sharp, granular sting that anchored him to the slick timber of the wharf. Harun had been his chief engineer for eleven years, a man whose left shoulder sat two inches lower than his right from hauling boiler pipes, a man who had gone down with the crushed stern of the *Bintang Laut* in the deep channel off Karimun. Jin had signed the maritime death declaration himself. He had watched the salvage barges abandon the wreck when the monsoon swells made diving impossible.

Yet here, registered thirty-four minutes ago in the digital clearinghouse of the Singapore receiver, was Harun’s personal provident fund account, accepting the debt-assignment rights to every mooring bollard and crane rail in Berth 9.

"Is it a mirror?" Lin Zhang whispered. She knelt beside him, her damp cotton shirt clinging to her collarbones, the smell of burnt battery acid and river mud rising from her hair. She reached toward the screen, her fingers twitching with a nervous, rhythmic flutter—one, two, three against her thigh, the old counting tic she used to drown out the hum of surveillance sweeps. "A shell trust? A dead man's identity bought off an admiralty salvage registry?"

"No," Jin rasped. His throat burned with the sulfurous tang of the back-siphoned harbor water. "The authorization key. Look at the trailing digits. Harun never used prime numbers for his security hash. He used the bearing angles of the Horsburgh Lighthouse. He said no machine algorithm would guess an old navigator’s compass error." He looked up, his gaze cutting through the greasy tropical drizzle toward the drydock. "He didn’t die in that stern section."

Behind them, the shipyard was stirring with a ugly, nervous heat. 

The high-pressure fire monitors had beaten back the tactical skiffs, but victory had brought no peace. Across the narrow pontoon bridge, the heavy iron gangway of Drydock 4 was groaning under the tread of dozens of boots. Four hundred stranded mariners, dock fitters, and fuel-depot workers were swarming up the scaffolding toward the weather deck of the *Pulai Indah*, the rusted, five-thousand-ton break-bulk freighter that sat propped on timber keel blocks like a slaughtered whale. 

They were soaked, shivering in the thirty-degree monsoon soup, and terrifyingly armed with spanners, iron pipe segments, and scrap plating. 

"They’re breaking the valve house padlocks," Chen Rui panted, jogging down the crane ramp. His forearms were wrapped in oily canvas strips to compress the flaming agony in his tendons. "The southern crews say we’re trapped like rats in a trench. They want to open the sea gate and flood the caisson so the receiver can’t bring salvage tugs into the inner basin. If they do that, the *Pulai Indah* will roll on her bilge keels and crush the bottom hull."

"They're panicking," Jin said, snapping the waterproof case shut and rising. His lumbar spine grated with a dry, sickening click that sent a white bolt of pain into his left heel. He leaned heavily on Rui’s shoulder for a fraction of a second, hiding the tremor, before catching his own balance. "If the ship rolls, we lose the tidal turbine cables running through her shaft alley. The whole yard goes dark by three in the morning."

"Then tell them that," Lin said, her breath shallow, her knuckles white against the shielded lantern. "Before someone throws an incendiary bottle into the bilge."

They crossed the dock floor in silence, the towering steel walls of the drydock rising forty feet above them, dripping with black kelp and barnacle crusts. High above, suspended between the gantry tracks, the storm clouds were bruised violet by the distant glare of the Jurong refinery flares across the strait.

On the main deck of the freighter, under the cavernous overhang of the forward crane house, the noise was deafening. 

Two men were shouting nose-to-nose over an open hatch cover. One was an Indonesian pump-man, his torso bare and stained with black bunker sludge; the other was a Singaporean marine electrician whose spectacles were tied to his ears with fishing twine. 

"We cut the shore cables now!" the pump-man screamed, slamming an open-ended wrench onto the steel plating. "When the harbor patrol comes back, they won't bring water nozzles! They'll bring legal injunctions and boarding cutters from the coast guard! If we’re wired to the mainland, they freeze our licenses by sunrise!"

"And if you cut the shore cables, the desalination plant stops!" the electrician yelled back, spitting through broken teeth. "My three children are drinking tank water that hasn't been boiled since Tuesday! You want us to drink harbor slime?"

A dozen voices roared in assent, another dozen roared in fury. The crowd surged, shoulder against wet shoulder, the raw somatic stink of fear, diesel exhaust, and unwashed wool suffocating under the tarp awning.

*CLANG.*

The sound was not an explosion, nor the report of a weapon. It was the sharp, mechanical strike of an engine-room telegraph gong, ringing out from the bridge wing.

Uncle Tan stood beside the brass pedestal, his swollen, arthritic hands resting on the curved wooden handle. The brass was green with verdigris, but the internal escapement was clean. The clockwork mechanism inside the housing ticked with a measured, inexorable clack-clack-clack.

"Five minutes," Uncle Tan called out. His voice was not loud, but it carried the gravelly density of sixty years in the yards, a voice that had cut through boiler room steam and typhoon squalls. "Article Four of the Covenant. The telegraph is set. The floor belongs to the watch."

The shouting sputtered. The pump-man wiped greasy sweat from his brow, glaring at the deck, his chest heaving. The electrician stepped back, breathing hard through his nose.

Jin climbed the ladder to the cargo hatch, the plastic flight case gripped in his right hand. He placed it squarely on the rusted iron coaming. He did not offer an apology, nor did he raise his voice in a rally. The rules were cut into the iron of the yard: five minutes of uninterrupted presentation, zero interruption, zero cross-talk until the brass chime fell.

"The skiffs were not coast guard," Jin said, the mechanical tick of the telegraph beating behind his words. "They were private recovery contractors hired by Euro-Asian Maritime Finance. They were repelled because our seawater monitors had more head-pressure than their hulls could take. But they left this."

He opened the case. The amber glow of the terminal lit the tight circle of faces: exhausted deckhands, young mothers holding infants wrapped in dry engine rags, aging crane operators with cataracts in their rheumy eyes.

"The warrant against Berth 9 has been bought," Jin said. "Not by the port authority. By an offshore trust operating under the maritime identity of Harun bin Idris."

A sharp murmur rippled through the older men. An oiler in the second row crossed himself. 

"Harun is dead," someone muttered. "The sea took him."

"His body was never recovered," Jin countered, his gaze sweeping the deck, refusing to let them look away. "And his trust just executed an administrative mortgage lien against this drydock. Whoever holds this terminal didn't come to sink us. They came to trigger an automated receivership default before dawn."

He pointed toward the narrow channel where the tidal turbines spun in the black depths.

"If we scatter into the mangroves in lifeboats, the trust assumes uncontested ownership of every kilowatt we generate. If we flood the dock to block them, we destroy our own shelter. That is what an algorithm wants: chaos that forces an abandonment order under the salvage codes. We have forty minutes before the tidal shift reverses. We do not run, and we do not break our own pumps."

The brass telegraph gave a sharp, metallic *ping*. 

The five minutes were up.

A heavy silence descended over the four hundred people on the deck. The rain pattered softly against the taut canvas above them, steady, cold, indifferent.

Uncle Tan reached into the wooden box beside the telegraph and drew the brass sortition drum forward. "Parity requires three," the old man said, his knuckles stiff as he spun the cylinder. Three numbered boxwood balls rattled within the perforated metal. "Three arbiters to inspect the log and confirm the course."

Uncle Tan opened the gate. Three wooden spheres dropped into his palm: *Nine. Twenty-seven. One hundred and three.*

Aisyah binti Rahman stepped forward from the shadows near the crane footing, her diving knife sheathed at her hip, her fingertips raw from high-voltage work. Behind her stepped a retired slipway master from Batam, and the young mother whose child was asleep against her collarbone.

Aisyah reached out, her scorched thumb brushing the edge of the tablet screen to verify the digital cryptographic ledger. 

Suddenly, the screen did not refresh its ledger.

The amber text flickered, collapsed into a single horizontal scan line, and flared blindingly violet.

A deep, pneumatic thud echoed from the bottom of the drydock beneath their boots.

The freighter lurched three inches to port with a sound like tearing sheet metal. Keel timbers shrieked under the sudden shifting of five thousand tons of deadweight. Far below, in the darkness beneath the hull, a high-volume sea valve was grinding open, throwing a massive geyser of harbor water against the concrete floor.

The terminal had not merely delivered an admiralty notice. 

It had executed a remote command line directly into the yard’s submerged pneumatic ballast manifolds—and the drydock was beginning to fill.

label: Chapter 9
title: Lin deploys Hague maritime liens against the private equity flotilla, paralyzing their legal insurance coverage
content:
The shudder did not travel through the air; it rose through the soles of their boots, a sickening, low-frequency grinding of five thousand tons of unballasted freighter scraping against aged concrete blocks.

"Sluice four!" Chen Rui shouted, his voice cracking on the spray. He was already over the railing, his boots sliding on the wet diamond-plate stairs. "They tripped the pneumatic release from the harbor channel!"

"Get the manual chokes!" Jin Wei barked. His lungs burned, raw from decades of inhaled bunker fumes, his collarbone throbbing where an old boiler flash had left the skin thick and hairless. He didn't look back at the four hundred faces huddled beneath the wind-whipped canvas awning. "Aisyah, take the south trench. Don't touch the hydraulic lines—they’ll be pressurized to two hundred bar. Dog down the mechanical spindles!"

Down in the basin, darkness was churning into froth. Seawater, black and smelling of harbor silt and decayed mangrove roots, geysered through the shattered pneumatic intake. The drydock was transforming into a drowning tank. If the water rose four feet before the keel wedges could be reset, the freighter would lose her balance, roll her bilge strakes against the concrete apron, and crush her own bottom plates.

Up in the gantry crane’s narrow control cab, sixty-five meters above the swirling foam, Lin Zhang leaned her forehead against the salt-streaked glass. Her temples hammered with a migraine so sharp it blurred her left eye. She dug into her pocket, found a brittle strip of dried tangerine peel—a childhood habit from the northern rail yards she had never broken—and pressed it between her teeth. The bitter citrus cut through the chemical stench of scorched insulation.

Her fingers did not touch the terminal’s main bus. That was what the maritime syndicate wanted: an exchange of packet requests that would allow their automated admiralty script to log an intentional sabotage event and revoke the yard’s safe-harbor status.

Instead, she plugged a shielded ribbon cable directly into the optical transmitter housing.

"Lin!" Chen Rui’s voice burst through the brass speaking tube near her ear, stripped of breath. "The lower valve seat is warped. Rust in the collar. We can’t close it with the handwheel—we need the yard gantry to drop the deadweight plug!"

"Five minutes," she whispered, her throat dry.

"We don't have five minutes!" Chen Rui yelled back, the metallic thrum of rushing water roaring in the background. "The tide is coming over the sill! If the skiffs outside ram the caisson gate now, the surge will rip the blocks clean out!"

Lin didn't answer. She opened the heavy, wax-sealed portfolio she had kept strapped to her ribs since Jakarta.

The syndicate wasn't fighting for the steel. They were fighting for the paper.

In international admiralty law, an offshore private equity flotilla did not move on diesel alone. Every interceptor skiff idling outside the harbor mouth, every armed contractor on their decks, operated under a mandatory web of indemnity: protection and indemnity policies underwritten through mutual clubs in London and Rotterdam, reinsured four times over through Singaporean clearinghouses. Without an active certificate of financial responsibility, no vessel could cross the boundary marker of a sovereign strait without rendering its master, its charterers, and its institutional lenders individually and criminally liable for maritime piracy and uninsured environmental hazard.

They thought the drydock was an abandoned asset. They thought the four hundred stranded mariners below were merely squatters without standing.

Lin brought up the terminal's air-gapped optical link. The cyan beam atop the crane shuddered against the torrential monsoon rain, its narrow wavelength fighting through sheets of tropical moisture toward the sister relay tower mounted on the abandoned grain silo three miles across the strait. Dropped packets flickered across her display—forty percent signal loss in the downpour. The salt air had pitted the outer lens, blooming the tight optical pencil into a ragged green smear.

She adjusted the manual focus dial with her left hand, feeling the coarse grit of salt corrosion grinding in the brass threads.

*Lock.*

She initiated the Hague Perpetual Asset Trust filing.

Not a protest. Not an appeal to a court that would take three years to read the first motion. It was a preemptive, automated maritime lien.

Under the Hague Trust protocols established during the Geneva sortition, the four hundred mariners living in Berth 9 were not passengers; they were legally registered possessory lienholders of the berth's kinetic infrastructure. Every hour they had spent scraping barnacles, every liter of bilge water they had pumped using their own salvaged battery banks, constituted an unpaid salvage wage under traditional maritime custom—a primary maritime lien that held absolute seniority over any corporate mortgage or bondholder syndicate.

Lin entered the biometric keys provided by the three sortition arbiters. Aisyah’s thumbprint. The Batam slipway master’s digital mark. The young mother’s cryptographic seal.

The ledger did not debate. It cross-referenced the global clearinghouse registries via the optical laser handshake, matching the hulls of the six private security interceptors idling outside the breakwater against the Lloyd’s Open Form casualty database.

*Transmitting.*

A gust of wind caught the gantry tower, swaying the cab six inches to the west. The optical link dropped to zero.

"Come on," Lin hissed through clenched teeth. Her vision swam with bright migraine aura. "Hold."

Down in the basin, the water was waist-deep on Chen Rui. He and Aisyah were knee-braced against an iron lever, shoving a half-ton solid steel drop-wedge into the intake conduit. Seawater hammered against Chen Rui’s ribs, cold and violently fast, threatening to rip his grip from the greasy iron.

"Drop it!" Aisyah screamed, her burned fingers slipping on the chain hoist. "Rui, let the dog fall!"

Chen slammed his shoulder into the trip lever. The wedge fell with a thunderous *clack*, biting into the intake rim. The geyser died instantly, choked to a churning boil of white foam, but the caisson seal behind them groaned. Outside, the wash of high-speed diesel engines reverberated through the steel gates.

The private equity flotilla was closing in, preparing to breach the dock.

Above them, the cyan laser found its mark through a brief tear in the rain clouds. The optical link locked green.

Lin Zhang depressed the transmit lever.

Across the Malacca Strait, fifty miles away in the glass towers of the financial district, the automated risk algorithms of three international maritime insurance syndicates processed the cryptographic filing.

A primary, non-subordinated wage and salvage lien was now recorded against the entire asset class of the private equity consortium, encumbering not just the drydock, but every auxiliary vessel under their corporate charter.

At sea, eight hundred yards from the drydock gate, the lead tactical interceptor was running at twenty-five knots, its searchlights slicing through the rain, aiming directly for the shipyard’s outer pontoon.

Inside the interceptor’s bridge, the master’s tactical navigation display did not go dark.

It turned amber, then solid crimson.

A synthesized audio tone chimed twice—the precise, neutral chime of a catastrophic underwriter cancellation. The vessel’s satellite-linked insurance transponder, tied to the London P&I registry, automatically revoked its voyage authorization. A block-freeze order flashed across the helm:

*INDEMNITY SUSPENDED. PRIMARY ADMIRALTY LIEN DETECTED. MASTER PERSONALLY LIABLE FOR ALL TRANSIT RISKS. AUTOMATED EMERGENCY SHUTDOWN IMMINENT.*

The contractor captain stared at the console, his hand freezing on the dual-throttle levers. If he advanced another fifty yards, his personal mariner’s license would be stripped, his family’s savings frozen in Singapore escrow, and his vessel classified as an uninsured rogue craft subject to immediate seizure by the regional coast guard.

"What is this?" the second officer stammered, pulling off his headset. "Did the company go into receivership?"

"No," the captain said, his voice flat, drained of all tactical swagger. "Someone just put a lien on our fuel tanks."

Slowly, reluctantly, the captain pulled the twin throttles back into neutral. Behind him, the five other interceptors saw his running lights drop and throttled back, drifting in the heavy monsoon swell, their engines idling in the dark.

In the crane cab, Lin watched the searchlights sweep harmlessly across the gray harbor water, turning slowly away from the caisson. She let out a long, shuddering breath, her forehead dropping back against the cold window. The salt on the glass was cold against her skin.

Then, from the depths of the drydock below, came a sound far worse than the roar of the sea valve.

It wasn't the hiss of an intake. It was the sharp, explosive *crack* of five-inch structural steel shearing under uneven lateral load.

The drydock hadn't leveled. The five thousand tons of the freighter had settled onto the blocks at a three-degree list. One of the forward concrete pillars, undermined by years of salt rot and the sudden deluge, had buckled.

A cloud of pulverized concrete dust puffed into the rain. The massive bow of the ship groaned, canting outward, its immense steel overhang tilting directly toward Berth 9—where four hundred men, women, and children stood trapped between the shifting hull and the sheer, thirty-foot drop of the seawall.

label: Chapter 10
title: Jin guides apprentice divers to repair an underwater fiber-optic conduit amidst dangerous 4-knot tidal currents
content:
The groan of Berth 9 did not stop. It deepened, rattling the calcium-crusted iron railings until the rust fell in gray snow. On the seawall apron, four hundred refugees shrank back against the concrete parapet, their breath misting in the torrential damp as the canted freighter’s bow hung over them like a cliff face waiting to drop.

Inside the caisson control trench, the drydock ballast lines stuttered.

"Conduit three is dead," Lin shouted from the pump well, her voice fighting the roar of the bilge discharge. Her skin was the color of curdled tallow, dark hollows bruised beneath her eyes from three sleepless rotations. "The foundation shift sheared the conduit trench outside the sluice gate. Telemetry to the seaward ballast valves is gone. If we can’t balance the starboard tanks before the tidal rip peaks, the keel blocks will roll."

Captain Jin Wei didn’t waste words on panic. Decades in the lower flats of rust-bucket bulkers had taught him that steel gave three distinct warnings before it killed you: first a hum, then a tick, then a silence. The ship was still ticking.

"Aisyah," Jin barked.

Aisyah binti Rahman was already hauling the vulcanized drysuits from the salt-stiffened lockers behind the workshop. Her fingers, scarred at the pads where high-voltage arcing had left white calluses, moved with furious efficiency across the brass inflator valves. Before she had ever touched an ROV tether, she had spent her adolescence free-diving for spiny lobsters off the coral shelves of Pulau Semakau; she gauged the channel's rip not by navigational buoys, but by the lateral torque pulling at the tendon behind her left knee.

"Four knots out there, Captain," she said, pulling a neoprene hood over her cropped hair. Her voice was flat, level, stripped of youth. "Current’s turning against the monsoon runoff. It’s washing machine water down by the sill."

"We go off the outer caisson catwalk," Jin said, dragging a heavy full-face mask over his neck. His lumbar spine flared with familiar, grinding pain—two crushed discs from an exploded steam line thirty years back that made bending feel like chewing glass. As a boy, before he ever went to sea, he had learned to calm the terror of dark water by humming sea shanties in four-four time, matching his lungs to the thrum of a diesel exhaust. He hummed now, low in his throat, a harsh, gravelly drone. "Conduit raceway is three meters below the mudline. We have twenty minutes of slack window before the strait floods."

Two apprentice divers, boys from the Batam boatyards who had never worked deeper than a harbor mooring, stood frozen by the dive staging rack, their eyes wide and white against their grease-smeared faces.

"Tether to me," Jin told them, his tone dropping into the mechanical cadence of survival. "Keep your fins off the gravel. If you get pinned against the intake grate, don't kick. Dump your suit gas. Drop to the mud. Roll left. Understand?"

The boys swallowed and nodded, their hands trembling as they buckled their lead-shot weight belts.

They dropped from the caisson's low service platform directly into the black throat of the channel.

The water didn't feel like liquid; it felt like a moving wall of cold wet cement. The Singapore Strait was emptying east to west, funneled between the granite riprap of the breakwater and the shipyard’s massive concrete caisson. At four knots, current ceased to be a drift—it became a hydraulic ram. It snatched Jin’s rubber-suited shoulders, slamming him hard against the guide wire before his buoyancy compensator could bite.

Silt blinded him instantly. The tropical sun, already suffocated by monsoon cloud, vanished beneath ten feet of churned, muddy brine laden with harbor runoff, decomposing mangrove pulp, and microscopic diesel droplets.

Through the bone-conduction comms clamped behind his ear, Lin’s voice crackled, distorted by the static of water: *"Jin... starboard ballast pressure rising... the cant is three point five degrees. You have twelve minutes before the crane tracks buckle."*

"On the guide," Jin grunted into his oral-nasal cup. "Aisyah. Left pin."

"Got it," her voice came back, tight, rhythmic with heavy breathing.

Their dive lamps cut yellow, cone-shaped tunnels through the murk, illuminating swarms of suspended silt that looked like driving sleet. Jin pulled himself hand-over-hand down the anchor chain. The cold seeped through his suit, biting his scarred collarbone where an old steam-scald had left the tissue thin and numb. Behind him, the two apprentice divers kicked frantically, their fins thrashing against the current, burning through their air at twice the safe consumption rate.

"Stop kicking!" Jin rasped, his voice raw from bunker cough. "Arm-haul only. Save your lung."

They reached the concrete sill twenty feet down. Here, the current compressed, howling through the gap beneath the drydock gate like an underwater gale. The roar was deafening—a deep, subsonic vibration that rattled Jin’s teeth inside his gums.

There lay the raceway: a rectangular trough cast into the granite foundation, meant to protect the armored umbilical that carried the drydock’s pulse.

It was smashed.

A ten-ton concrete scour-block, dislodged by the listing freighter’s shuddering keel blocks above, had toppled directly across the steel conduit tray. The three-inch armored casing—sheathing two hundred strands of pure glass—was crushed flat beneath forty cubic feet of mossy aggregate. The outer steel braiding had peeled open like an overcooked sausage, its broken fiber cores trailing in the current like pale, severed horsehair.

"Crushed," Aisyah said, dropping to her knees on the slime-covered ledge. The current caught her dive cylinder, trying to flip her over the drop-off into the sixty-foot channel trench, but she jammed her heavy brass pry-bar into an expansion seam and held. "Zero continuity. Casing pinched clear to the copper sheath."

"Jack," Jin commanded, pointing his beam at the narrow crevice beneath the scour-block.

The first apprentice fumbled with the canvas tool bag. A brass-bodied hydraulic spread-jack slipped from his neoprene glove, tumbling toward the abyss. Jin’s hand shot out—instinct older than his pain—and snagged the high-pressure hose by two fingers, dragging the tool back with a jolt that sent an electric spike through his injured lower back. He didn't curse. Cursing cost air.

"Seat it," Jin ordered, thrusting the tool into Aisyah’s hands. "Under the rebar. Lift two inches. That’s all we need to pull the slack loop."

Aisyah wedged the flat jaws of the spreader into the narrow crack beneath the granite mass. She began pumping the manual lever. *Clack. Clack. Clack.*

The tool groaned under the strain, hydraulic fluid weeping past its salt-scored seals. Slowly, agonizingly, the concrete slab shifted, peeling up an inch from the steel trough. A plume of black, foul-smelling anaerobic mud puffed out, carried instantly away by the four-knot current.

"Slack coming!" Jin yelled, gesturing to the second apprentice. "Pull the green sleeve! Don't kink it!"

The boy reached into the recess, his fingers clumsy with fear. He hauled out the yellow emergency splice enclosure—an air-gapped, gel-filled junction box designed to be bridged underwater using mechanical splice blocks. But the cable had torn short. The factory terminal block was mangled, brass pins sheared off flush against the polyurethane boot.

"No connector," Aisyah panted, her breathing ragged in the mask. "We have to core-splice. Cold-cure resin."

Jin looked at his wrist gauge. Seven minutes of slack water left. When the tide turned fully, the reverse surge from the deep-water shipping channel would sweep this ledge with five knots of unyielding hydrodynamic force. No human grip could hold a pry-bar in that.

"Open the gel cassette," Jin said.

His fingers were thick, stiffened by age and salt, but inside the rubber diving mitts, the muscle memory remained. He stripped his outer gloves, exposing his bare skin to the biting, grease-slicked water. His fingers turned white in seconds, the cold deadening the nerves until he could barely feel the micro-thin glass strands.

Working inside the small canvas shelter-hood Aisyah held over the work site to break the flow of the current, Jin began cleaving the fiber ends with a manual ceramic blade.

One strand. Blue to blue.

*Click.*

Lin’s voice in his ear was frantic now: *"Hull list at four degrees! The refugee barricade is cracking, Jin! Berth nine is going!"*

"Shut up, Lin," Jin whispered, his breath whistling through his teeth.

Two strands. Orange to orange.

The current hammered the hood. Aisyah’s shoulder slammed against Jin’s helmet, but she didn't give an inch, wedging her knees into the concrete seam until the vulcanized rubber tore against the barnacles, sea-water flooding her left leg. She didn't make a sound. She just held the canvas.

Three strands. Green to green.

*Click.*

The tiny LED on the junction cassette flickered from amber to faint, pulsing cyan.

"Continuity!" Lin screamed over the comms. "Starboard three valve responding! Ballast pumps kicking—we're taking on water forward! She’s leveling!"

A great, hydraulic shudder ran through the caisson wall as the five-thousand-ton hull shifted back toward an even keel, the sound vibrating through the water like an earthquake.

Jin reached to snap the heavy waterproof clamps over the resin casing.

Then, from the channel abyss directly behind them, the current stopped dead.

Not a natural slack. The water went completely still for three heartbeats—then sucked violently *seaward*, dragging Jin, Aisyah, and the apprentice divers toward the deep navigation trench as a massive, low-frequency hum vibrated through the bedrock beneath their fins.

Something enormous had just entered the narrow channel mouth without navigation lights, displacing tens of thousands of tons of water in a single, blind surge.

label: Chapter 11
title: Food supplies tighten; Uncle Tan organizes saltwater aquaponics in repurposed ballast tanks
content:
The outward surge dragged Jin’s boots off the caisson rim, throwing his weight against the safety lanyard with a violence that popped the stitching along his harness. In the black churn of the channel mouth, the deadweight super-freighter slid past without a single running light, a wall of slab-sided steel five storeys high displacing tens of thousands of tons of deep water as it coasted on its own momentum toward the sandbar. It was not firing. It did not need to. It simply dropped both bow anchors into the navigation channel with a grinding roar that shook the seabed, slewing across the fairway to choke off the last open approach to Berth Nine.

Jin kicked against the undertow, his left knee screaming where old cartilage had ground to powder. He hooked his forearm under Aisyah’s collar, dragging her back into the shelter of the concrete footing. Her suit was ripped from hip to calf, the cold brine already leaching the color from her skin, but she still clamped both hands around the fiber-splice box, pressing it to her chest like a newborn.

Above them, on the crane gantry, Lin Zhang’s voice crackled through the ear-piece, pinched with terror: *"The fairway is blocked. They’ve dropped a four-hundred-meter hulk across the shallows. No supply skiffs are getting through from the islands. Jin, we’re corked."*

"Get the ladder," Jin rasped into the dead microphone of his mask, his throat raw with the taste of sulfur and heavy fuel. He spat a mouthful of oily foam into the scuppers as they broke the surface beside the slipway. "Lin. The rope."

Ten minutes later, they stood dripping on the iron plates of the fabrication shed. The monsoon heat slammed into them like a wet wool blanket, forty degrees of swamp air turning the salt crust on their skin into an itching paste.

Berth Nine was starving, and the four hundred and twelve mariners sheltered in its cavernous guts already knew it.

Inside the old mess deck, beneath overhead beams painted in flaking lead primer, the air smelled of scorched vinegar and stale sweat. Three hundred men and women—Burmese deckhands, Indonesian grease-wipers, laid-off crane operators from the container terminals—sat along the trestle benches. In front of each lay a plastic bowl containing three ounces of split peas, boiled until the skins split, and two dry biscuits gray with pantry weevils.

At the head of the galley counter, a shouting match had flared between two tug engineers over a five-gallon plastic drum of cooking oil. One had a rusted pry-bar raised; the other held an iron ladle like a truncheon.

*Clang.*

The brass telegraph bell above the scullery door rang once.

The sound was small, dry, and deliberate. Uncle Tan stood beside the bulkhead, one swollen hand resting on the counter-weight lever. He was seventy-one, his spine curved like a ship’s rib after a grounding, his fingers misshapen by decades of monsoon dampness that turned his knuckles into knobby ginger roots. As a boy in the swamp kampongs of the Kallang Basin, before the government had dredged the creeks and poured concrete over the mangrove nurseries, he had caught fighting crickets in wooden matchboxes, learning to judge the wetness of the mud simply by pressing his palm against the bank in the dark. He carried no clipboard, no megaphone. He wore only a stained cotton undershirt and faded blue drill trousers rolled above his shins.

"Five minutes," Tan said softly. His voice did not carry the bark of a bosun, but it cut through the room’s hot, stagnant air with the weight of someone who had seen three shipping empires dissolve into bankruptcy auctions. "Telegraph says cool down. Put the iron down, boys. The iron doesn't feed nobody."

The engineer with the pry-bar stared at him, chest heaving, veins standing out on his neck like hemp lines. For four seconds, nobody breathed. Then the younger man’s shoulders dropped, the tool hitting the linoleum with a dull thud.

"They cut the Batam run, Uncle," the engineer muttered, wiping his wet face on his sleeve. "The market barges won't cross the fairway with that bulk-ship sitting in the channel. Two days. That's what’s in the dry stores. Then what? We eat rust?"

"We eat what the sea gives," Tan said. He turned and pointed a crooked finger toward the dark, cavernous hollow beneath Berth Nine's drydock floor. "Grab the scrap scrapers. Bring the lye tubs. We have six thousand tons of empty iron downstairs."

Beneath the slipway lay the hull of the *Heng Shan*, an abandoned thirty-year-old bulk ore carrier that the port receivers had left to rot when her owners folded in the tanker crash of '18. Her bottom plates sat flat on the keel blocks, her twin starboard ballast tanks—each forty meters long, eight meters deep, designed to swallow twelve thousand tons of dirty seawater to balance an empty crossing—hollow as cathedral tombs.

By midnight, sixty mariners were down in the belly of Tank Port-Four.

The heat inside the enclosed steel was suffocating, thick with the stench of thirty years of anaerobic mud, dried fuel residue, and dead barnacles. Portable floodlights run off the tidal turbine's night-cycle battery cast harsh, blinding glare against the rust-scaled frames. Jin Wei swung an iron scraper against the bulkhead, his lower back knotting into a hard, fiery spasm with every stroke. Flakes of red scale peeled away, falling into the bilge water around his boots in sharp, metallic sheets.

"Not down to bare metal," Tan shouted from the access hatch, his knees clicking as he climbed down the vertical rung ladder one rung at a time, testing each steel rod with his weight before trusting it. "You scrub to the plate, the raw iron bleeds oxide into the water! The gills choke in six hours! Just knock off the slime and the petroleum crust! Then the lime wash!"

Aisyah was already wading through the knee-deep black slurry at the tank’s aft end, dragging a flexible suction hose salvaged from the bilge pumps. Her eyes were red-rimmed, ringed with dark grease, her temple bruised where the dive-rig had slammed her against the caisson, but she moved with cold, mechanical economy. Every ten minutes, the suction strainer clogged on a knot of decayed rope or thick bunker sludge; every ten minutes, she plunged her bare hands into the foul water, cleared the mesh, and cursed in quiet, steady Malay.

"We have no freshwater to fill this," Jin said, pausing to lean against his scraper, his chest rattling as he fought for breath in the damp air. "Even if Lin keeps the reverse-osmosis stack running on the tidal trickle, that’s four tons a day. We need three hundred tons just to float the bio-filters."

Tan reached into the pocket of his trousers and pulled out a fistful of dark, waxy green leaves. He crushed them between his palms, holding them under Jin’s nose.

The smell was sharp, brackish, rich with the rot of estuarine peat.

"Mangrove apple," Tan said. "Avicennia marina. Black mangrove shoots. The boys took the work-skiff into the drainage canals behind the old cement works this afternoon. Pulled two hundred seedlings out of the mudflats. They drink sea brine, Jin. They sweat the salt out through the back of their leaves like an old stoker."

He gestured toward the long, tiered staging racks the shipyard carpenters were already bolting to the tank’s interior ribs using angle-iron sliced from scrapped container flats.

"We don't desalt the water," Tan said, kneeling down and dipping his hand into the shallow channel they had carved through the center of the tank floor. He tasted the residue on his finger, his weathered face tightening as he gauged the silt. "We run the high-tide surge through the sea-chests, through two gravel beds to drop the harbor grit. Then the mangrove roots take the ammonia. We put the sea bass fingerlings from the river fish-traps on the lower tier. Tilapia in the middle. Mangrove greens on top. We don't ask the dry land for a single grain of rice."

"The water is hot, Uncle," Aisyah said, hauling the cleared hose to the next frame. "The hull plates sit in thirty-five-degree mud outside. Sea bass boil in that."

"Not when the tide runs," Tan replied. He tapped the thick steel skin of the hull with his knuckles. "Six hours in, six hours out. The channel current pulls fifteen knots of deep, cold bottom-water past this plate twice a day. We plumb the intake low, through the old sea-suction valves on the bottom floor. The sea becomes our radiator."

It was grueling, brutal work, devoid of grace. There were no digital readouts to tell them if the chemical balance was true. They relied on Tan’s tongue to measure the salt, on the smell of the bilge wash to know when the caustic soda had neutralized the fuel oil, and on the blistered hands of eighty starving sailors working by the yellow glow of work-lights to assemble two hundred meters of perforated PVC pipe.

By four in the morning, the first wash-water was drained. The twin ballast tanks gleamed dull gray under a fresh coat of slaked agricultural lime. Above the tanks, suspended from the cross-beams, rows of broad-spectrum LED strips salvaged from refrigerated fruit containers flickered on, casting a violent, magenta dawn across the rust-streaked steel.

In the shallow, aerated water of the lower troughs, forty dozen small, silver-scaled estuary bass—netted from the industrial runoff creeks by the younger deckhands during the slack tide—darted between the submerged bundles of mangrove roots.

Jin sat on an overturned chemical bucket at the edge of the tank, his palms raw, his spine locked in a dull, thrumming ache that radiated into his thighs. Across the tank, mariners were leaning over the iron rails, their faces bathed in the strange purple light, watching the small fish turn in the clear, brackish wash. For the first time in six days, nobody was shouting. The silence inside the ship’s iron belly was broken only by the rhythmic, bubbling hiss of the compressed-air lines.

Then, through the twenty-millimeter steel plate of the bulk carrier’s bottom hull, came a sound.

It was not the slap of the tide.

It was a heavy, metallic *thunk*, followed by the distinct, high-frequency whine of an underwater hydraulic core-drill biting into the steel plate directly beneath their feet.

Jin froze. Tan’s hand went still on the water valve.

A second *thunk* echoed through the framing, sixty feet forward, accompanied by the magnetic clatter of a heavy hull-crawler locking onto the exterior keel. The receiver's tactical salvage crews had not waited for starvation to do their work. They were under the hull, boring into the ballast intake chests to flood the drydock before the morning assembly could convene.

label: Chapter 12
title: Act I Climax: Corporate gunboats deploy electronic jamming; the optical laser link pierces the cloud layer to Node 2 (Alps) and Node 1 (Detroit)
content:
The grinding bite of tungsten carbide against the ship’s bottom plating sent a shudder straight up Jin Wei’s shinbones. It was not an explosion, but something far more intimate: a cold, hydraulic boring through the dead-center of sea chest three. 

“Aisyah!” Jin’s voice was a gravel rasp, stripped of breath by the sudden spasm in his lumbar spine. 

Aisyah was already moving. Her fingers, scarred white across the pads from an alternator flash burn, caught the four-foot cheater pipe resting against the tank framing. She didn’t speak. Under the violet glare of the grow-lights, her skin was slick with sweat and foul bilge mud. She rammed the pipe over the handle of the sea-chest emergency flapper valve and threw all forty-eight kilos of her frame against the lever.

Through the hull, the magnetic crawler hummed like a nest of hornets. 

*Clack-clack-clack.* The brass flapper swung inward, fighting the outward rush of displaced air, then slammed home against its neoprene seat with a dull, wet thud that vibrated through the marrow of Jin’s teeth. Beneath them, the core-drill screeched as it hit the backed bronze plate, shuddered, and sheared its bit with an ear-splitting snap. 

Silence fell across the ballast floor, save for the frantic darting of the silver estuary bass among the submerged mangrove roots. 

Then the radio on Jin’s harness died.

It did not click off; it dissolved into a violent, hissing wash of carrier hash. A wide-band RF carpet sweep. 

“They’re in the channel,” Uncle Tan wheezed from the access ladder. The old man’s knuckles were swollen to the size of walnuts, his knees trembling as he took the iron rungs one at a time. “No horn, no running lights. Skiffs. Three of them, hugging the caisson shadow.”

Jin hauled himself up the vertical ladder, his vertebrae grinding like coarse sand in a gearbox. He had grown up on the muddy flats of Pulau Ubin, where the smell of incoming rain always brought the scent of salted duck eggs drying on bamboo mats behind his mother’s kitchen; now, the air entering his lungs tasted solely of vaporized heavy fuel oil, ozone, and the electric sulfur of a closing monsoon front.

He broke onto the open weather deck of Berth 9 into a wall of falling water. 

The tropical squall had hit with the weight of an overturned lake. Torrents of warm rain swept sideways across the slipway, drumming against the steel skin of stacked containers. Out in the black chop of the traffic lane, two miles south, the running lights of three commercial gunboats churned the water into frothing phosphorus. They were running an interdiction perimeter, blacking out every civilian frequency from here to the Johor coast.

Sixty-five meters above the slipway, perched in the exposed maintenance cage of the gantry crane, Dr. Lin Zhang clutched the rusted guardrail with both hands.

Her eyes burned behind salt-streaked glasses. The migraine that had lived behind her left eyebrow for three days was now a hot spike driven through her temple. Below her, the shipyard was a dark labyrinth of wet iron; above her, the sky was an impenetrable roof of violet-black thunderheads. 

Beside her, Chen Rui knelt in three inches of standing rainwater on the crane platform, his forearms wrapped tightly in strips of black bicycle inner-tube to keep the inflamed tendons from tearing off the bone. His hands gripped the vernier adjustment wheels of the optical transceiver—a salvaged telescope barrel fitted with high-gain cyan emitter diodes, seated on an old surveyor’s leveling plate.

“The jammers took the UHF backhaul!” Lin yelled into the gale, her voice ripped away by the wind. She leaned over Chen’s shoulder, reciting prime numbers under her breath—*seventeen, nineteen, twenty-three*—the only mental tether keeping the height and the panic from emptying her stomach over the rail. “No telemetry from the tugs. The harbor mesh is severed.”

“Don’t need the radio!” Chen shouted back, spitting rain from his cracked lips. “Look at the meter!”

Lin wiped her glasses on her soaked shirt, smearing grease across the glass. The analog needle on the transceiver’s quadrant detector was twitching, dying, leaping back to zero. Salt crust was already fouling the quartz window. The heavy rain was scattering ninety percent of the light, turning the transceiver’s focused beam into a useless, diffused green glow that illuminated nothing but falling raindrops.

Down at the water level, the first tactical skiff struck the caisson.

The sound was a hard, rubberized slap against the outer timber fenders, followed instantly by the metallic bite of grappling grapnels catching the edge of the dock gate. Men in dark neoprene armor, devoid of flags or insignia, were hauling themselves up the wet timber pilings, carrying pneumatic cutters to breach the main sluice locks. If they dropped the caisson gate, four million gallons of harbor sludge would rush into Berth 9, capsizing the bulk carrier on its keel blocks and drowning three hundred families in the lower holds.

“Monitors!” Jin bellowed through a salvaged brass megaphone from the bridge wing. “Tan! Man the monitors!”

Uncle Tan didn’t run. His legs wouldn't let him. He leaned his entire body weight into the bronze wheel of the salvaged salvage-pump manifold. 

With a hollow, thundering groan that shook the pier, the twin tidal-fed fire pumps kicked in. Seawater, drawn straight from the four-knot channel rip, surged through the four-inch deck pipes. 

At the drydock rim, two dock hands seized the twin monitor nozzles. A solid column of green ocean water, roaring under two hundred pounds of pressure, smashed through the dark. It hit the lead boarding skiff not as spray, but as an iron bar. The vessel dipped violently, rolled forty degrees on its beam ends, and took fifty barrels of harbor water over the gunwales in four seconds. The boarding ladders tore free, spilling two tactical operatives into the foaming slipway, their heavy gear dragging them under until their auto-inflating vests violently popped them back to the surface, gasping and disoriented in the blinding wash.

The second monitor opened up, laying down a blinding curtain of heavy sea mist directly across the intruders' infrared sights, turning their thermal optics into a wall of useless gray soup.

Up on the crane, the wind sheared violently from the northeast.

“The mirror's loose!” Chen cried out. His wrench slipped on a corroded bronze bolt, stripping the skin from his knuckles. “The wind load is turning the gantry head! I can't hold the azimuth!”

Lin didn’t think. She threw her hip against the heavy steel housing of the optical barrel, pinning her small, shivering frame between the shuddering machine and the cold iron truss of the crane. The sharp edge of a mounting bracket cut through her linen shirt, slicing into her ribs. The pain was sudden, sharp, and cold.

*Twenty-nine, thirty-one, thirty-seven.*

“Turn it!” she screamed, her breath catching in her throat as the blood ran warm down her side, immediately washed thin by the downpour. “Rui, crank the declination! Three degrees up! The cloud ceiling is breaking over the channel!”

Chen Rui locked his bleeding hands onto the brass vernier. His muscles knotted, his teeth bared in a grimace of pure agony as the tendonitis fired white-hot along his arms. He forced the barrel up against the shrieking crosswind. One notch. Two notches.

Between two boiling banks of monsoon clouds, a narrow, jagged rift opened—a vertical chimney in the storm where the pressure dropped and the stars burned like ice through the thinning vapor.

“Now!” Lin choked out. “Fire the emitter!”

Chen dropped the manual knife-switch.

A needle of pure, concentrated cyan light stabbed out from the crane tower. 

It was not a radio wave that could be choked by Aegis-Omni’s carrier jammers; it was a physical lance of coherent photons. It sliced through the churning sea mist, pierced the eye of the cloud rift, and shot straight into the high-altitude atmospheric inversion.

For three agonizing heartbeats, the receiver needle on the quadrant meter lay dead against the stop-pin. 

Then, two thousand miles to the northwest, bounced from the orbital mirrors and caught by the cold granite spine of the Swiss Alps, the return carrier struck back. 

A pulse of deep, invisible infrared light answered the cyan beam. 

On Chen’s portable diagnostic screen, wrapped in clear plastic to keep off the salt rain, the raw terminal stream erupted into life. Not in graphics, not in corporate interfaces, but in a relentless, cascading waterfall of cryptographically verified ledger blocks. Detroit’s foundries. The Alpine hydro-penstocks. Berth 9’s battery banks. The three isolated nodes struck a single, immutable triangle of consensus across the curve of the dark planet.

The air on the crane platform smelled suddenly of scorched quartz and ozone.

Down below, on the slipway, the second Apex gunboat cut its searchlights. The tactical skiffs, wallowing half-submerged in the wash of the fire monitors, cut their grapnel lines and fell back into the boiling channel, their crews dragging their sodden boarding teams from the rip.

Lin slumped against the gantry rail, her ribcage throbbing, her chest heaving as she pulled the thick, wet sea air into her lungs. Chen fell back onto the rusted deck plates, his forearms locked in rigid, trembling cramps.

Jin Wei lowered his megaphone on the bridge wing. His knuckles were gray from gripping the rail. A ragged cheer, muffled by the rain, rose from the dark lower deck where the mariners stood watch.

Then, from the outer roads beyond the breakwater, a sound rolled across the water.

It was not the high whine of a skiff’s outboard. It was the deep, seismic, three-tone blast of an ocean-going salvage tug’s horn.

Through the curtains of falling rain, Jin saw them. 

Not tactical skiffs. Not light private craft. 

Rounding the northern light, two massive, black-hulled maritime enforcement cutters—each displacing three thousand tons, their bows reinforced with steel collision wedges—steamed abreast into the channel, their wake flattening the chop as their searchlights ignited simultaneously, locking their blinding beams directly onto the iron gates of Berth 9.

label: Chapter 13
title: The naval blockade tightens across the international traffic separation scheme
content:
The twin enforcement cutters did not charge the slipway; they did something far worse. They throttled down to five knots, their reinforced steel collision bows carving two curling, slate-colored trenches into the chop, and swung abreast across the mouth of the channel.

The sudden backwash slammed against the rusted caisson gates of Berth 9 with the concussive thump of a depth charge. Deep in the drydock’s belly, three thousand tons of seawater surged against the concrete sills, rattling the timber shoring until the iron drift-pins screamed in their housings.

Jin Wei clamped his molars down on a bitter clove leaf, an old habit from his early days as a deck boy when bunker oil seeped into every ration of rice. The raw spice stung the roof of his mouth, cutting through the reek of ozone and scorched quartz drifting from the gantry tower above. 

"They aren't boarding," he muttered into the salt spray.

Beside him on the bridge wing, Uncle Tan adjusted his grip on the rusted iron railing, his swollen knuckles whitening under the strain. The old mariner squinted through the halogen glare lancing off the lead cutter’s flying bridge, watching the rhythmic pitch of its rounded bow. 

"Riding high forward," Tan rasped, his voice scraping like gravel tossed in an empty drum. "Look at the red lead on her waterline. She’s dumped her forepeak ballast to clear the southern shallows. She’s skittish in a cross-rip, Jin. She’s built to intimidate, not to fight the tide."

High above them, sixty-five meters in the air, the wind was an open hand shoving the crane platform toward the channel. 

Lin Zhang pressed her shoulder hard against the steel upright of the optical transceiver housing, her thumbs hammering a silent, rapid count against the brass buckles of her harness—three, five, seven, eleven—the old reflex she had relied on through endless fluorescent nights in the university’s lower sub-basement when the ventilation failed and panic threatened to close her windpipe.

"Link’s fading," she called down through the crane’s sound-powered telephone, her voice snatched away by the squall before it reached the horn. She hauled the handset back to her mouth, shouting directly into the brass diaphragm. "Chen! Rain scatter is eating the beam! Optical degradation is past forty percent!"

On the platform deck behind her, Chen Rui was down on his knees in a pool of foul bilge water, ignoring the salt spray soaking through the shoulders of his canvas smock. He leaned his face within two inches of the open junction box, his eyes narrowed, his nose twitching as he sniffed the rubberized seals. It was a nervous compulsion he had picked up in the refit yards of Pasir Panjang—burnt copper and overheating neoprene carried distinct scents long before an instrument needle flickered toward zero. 

"The mirrors are tracking!" Chen yelled, his forearms locked in stiff, aching tremors from wrestling the manual elevation gearing against the gale. "The Alpine node is holding the high-orbit bounce, but the photons are smearing against the downpour! If the cutters throw their wash into our line of sight, the whole packet stream collapses!"

Through the binoculars, Jin saw the lead vessel’s deck crew moving in tight, yellow-slickered teams. They were not unlimbering boarding ladders or preparing grapple mortars. Instead, two hydraulic cranes swung out over the cutter’s stern, lowering massive, segmented steel cylinders linked by heavy steel mesh into the churning water.

Floating containment booms. Industrial, harbor-grade interdiction barriers designed to corral burning tanker slicks—or to hermetically seal a contaminated berth.

A voice cut through the drumming squall, blasted from the cutter’s bridge-wing hailer. It was flat, mechanical, and scrubbed of anger—the unyielding cadence of an admiralty receiver reading from a legal script.

*"Berth Nine vessel and drydock complex. You are in direct violation of the Malacca Strait Traffic Separation Scheme. Under international admiralty injunction and port safety authority decree, your facility is designated an unnavigable hazard. A protective cordon is being established. Stand down all unmonitored power generation and prepare for harbor master mooring inspection."*

"Unnavigable hazard," Jin spat, the clove leaf pulp bitter on his tongue. "They aren't storming the gates because they don't have to. They’re walling us in."

A wet, dripping hand slapped down onto the bridge-wing scupper. 

Aisyah hauled herself over the gunwale, shedding salt water like an otter. She collapsed onto one knee, chest heaving, the black neoprene of her diving suit slick with grease from the outer pilings. She reached down with a trembling thumb to touch the smooth river stone she kept wedged inside the sheath of her dive knife—a rounded piece of quartz she had pulled from her family's drowned kelong traps years before the mega-terminals had dredged the sandbars out from under them.

"They're dropping sinkers," she gasped, her voice raw from breathing compressed air through a pitted regulator. She coughed, spitting a mouthful of briny phlegm onto the steel deck. "Two heavy chain drags... right across the deep trench. They’re pinning the outer perimeter."

Jin leaned over her, his hand gripping her shoulder. "The channel turbines?"

"Not yet," Aisyah panted, pointing a gloved finger out toward the churning gray rip where the tidal current boiled past the point. "The chains are fifty yards upstream. But the drag lines are weighted with dead-weight scrap. When the tide turns in forty minutes... the sweep will drag those lines right into the turbine runners. If the blades foul under full tidal torque, the main shafts will twist like licorice."

Without the tidal turbines anchored in the channel bed, the shipyard was dead. 

The salvaged battery banks in Drydock 4 could carry the internal mesh and the bilge pumps for twelve hours, maybe fourteen. But without the heavy current of the channel driving the generators, the reverse-osmosis desalination plant would seize. Three hundred mariners and dockers, bottled up behind a steel-mesh curtain with the monsoon salt fouling every freshwater cistern, would be drinking brackish sludge before tomorrow’s dusk.

"They want us to shut down the water intake ourselves," Jin said, the chill of the realization sinking deep into his belly. "No shots fired. No martyrs for the foreign press. Just twenty-four hours of dry throats and a fouled turbine, and we invite their tugs in to tow us out to the scrap anchorage."

From the top of the gantry, Lin’s shout cracked through the sound-powered telephone.

"Jin! Look at the second cutter! Look at her stern!"

Jin lifted his glasses. The second vessel, the smaller of the two enforcement craft, had backed down into the lee of the outer breakwater. Her crew wasn't setting booms. A heavy, braided steel towing pendant, thick as a man's thigh, was being payed out from a massive hydraulic drum on her afterdeck. At the end of the cable, a heavy three-pronged grappling anchor swung from a derrick.

They were not trying to hook the iron caisson gates. The gates were anchored into fifty thousand tons of pre-stressed concrete. 

They were lining up on the base of the gantry crane.

"The crane's footing," Jin whispered, the blood draining from his weathered face. 

The crane was an antique, riding on twin steel rails laid down four decades ago to service panamax container hulls. Its south bogies were pinned to the seawall, less than twenty paces from the open water. If the cutter snagged the lower truss with that towing hawser and backed her twin diesels into the six-knot ebb, the lateral shear would tear the mounting pins from the wet concrete. 

The sixty-five-meter tower would topple like a severed pine straight into the harbor channel, taking the optical transceiver, the laser link, and Lin and Chen with it.

"Uncle Tan!" Jin barked, his voice dropping all hesitation. "Get below to the ballast manifold! Man the manual valves on the seaward ballast tank! Aisyah, take two runners from the boiler gang—divert the steam return line from the auxiliary turbine straight into the fire monitor headers!"

Aisyah blinked, wiping salt from her lashes. "The monitor pumps can't reach their bridge from here, Jin. The wind's against us."

"We aren't aiming for their bridge," Jin said grimly. "We’re blinding their helm. Uncle Tan—when I drop the gantry wedge, I want forty tons of harbor water dumped into the south caisson. Drop the dock's bow three degrees. Pull the crane's rail below the wash line."

Tan’s eyes widened, then a slow, yellow-toothed grin broke across his weathered face. "The hawser won't bite if the truss is under three feet of surf. It'll slide right off the iron."

"Go!" Jin roared.

On the gantry above, the wind screeched through the cross-bracing. 

Lin stood poised on the narrow maintenance grating, her hands locked around the manual aiming yoke of the laser transceiver. The lead cutter had turned its forward searchlight bank directly into the crane cab, bathing the steel platform in a blinding, white-hot glare that washed out every reference point against the black horizon. 

Beside her, Chen was screaming over the howling squall, pointing toward the channel.

The second cutter had gunned its diesels. A thick plume of black exhaust erupted from its low-profile stacks. The three-pronged grappling anchor plunged into the foam forty feet off the slipway, its heavy chain paying out with a sound like tearing sheet metal.

The cable snapped taut. 

The gantry tower shuddered beneath their boots with a sickening, metallic groan. Two of the three-inch steel drift pins holding the southern rail shoe sheared off with reports like rifle cracks, the broken bolts whistling through the night air and splashing into the dark water below.

The entire sixty-five-meter crane tilted two degrees to the seaward, throwing Lin violently against the safety railing. 

The optical beam to the Alps snapped. 

On the diagnostics screen beside Chen’s knees, the green stream of cryptographically verified blocks froze, hitched, and died.

Down on the water, the cutter’s twin screws thrashed the harbor into boiling foam, the tow-line rising dripping and rigid out of the black sea, pulling the ancient iron tower inch by agonizing inch toward the edge of the abyss.

label: Chapter 14
title: Predatory banks declare the terminal an illegal salvage operation; Lin executes a reciprocal usufruct cargo swap with Chilean lithium nodes
content:
The safety harness bit into Lin’s ribs as the gantry lurched, the steel catwalk slanting under her boots like the deck of a foundering barge. Below, the hawser hummed with catastrophic tension, vibrating so violently it sprayed an aerosol of seawater off its braided strands.

"Jin!" Chen screamed, his knuckles white around the railing, his thumb clamped between his teeth until the skin split. "The truss is twisting! If the lower shoe goes, the whole tower rolls into the slipway!"

Lin didn't shout. Her breath came in shallow, ragged hitches, the copper taste of a panic attack coating her tongue. Her vision flared at the periphery—the telltale shimmering zigzag of an oncoming migraine brought on by forty straight hours staring through optical collimators. With her free hand, she pressed a blunt thumbnail deep into the tendon of her left wrist, an old habit from her youth in the suffocating aisles of her mother’s textile stockroom, grounding herself in localized pain to stop her vision from tunneling to black.

Sixty meters down, the dock responded.

A low, hydraulic thud reverberated through the hollow caissons. Uncle Tan had dropped the south ballast valve. Harbor water, black and thick with river silt, surged into the lower chambers. The dock's seaward edge sagged instantly, dipping three degrees into the swell.

At the same instant, a deafening hiss tore through the rain. Aisyah threw the diverted bypass. High-pressure steam from the auxiliary turbine slammed into the fire monitor lines, mixing with the raw saltwater feed. What erupted from the forward nozzles was not a clean jet, but a roaring, boiling blizzard of scalding fog and vaporized spray.

The wind caught the plume, rolling it directly into the cutter’s wheelhouse.

Through the whiteout, the cutter’s searchlights scattered into a blinding, featureless haze. Blind at the helm and caught off-balance as the dock’s iron truss dipped beneath the surging surf, the cutter’s pilot sheared hard to port to avoid grounding on the slipway sill. 

The tow-line slackened by an inch. It was all the physics needed.

With a shriek of tearing zinc, the greased grappling fluke lost its purchase on the submerged iron beam. The cable whipped free with the crack of a snapped bullwhip, slicing across the water and leaving a smoking furrow of white froth before sinking into the channel. 

The 65-meter crane snapped back against its remaining structural stops. The impact rattled Lin’s teeth in her skull; her head cracked against the transceiver mount, sending stars cascading across her eyes.

"Clear!" Jin’s voice rasped through the copper voice-pipe from the lower quay, thick and wet with his chronic bunker-oil cough. "Hawser slipped! Aisyah, kill the steam before you melt the pump gaskets!"

The roar died, replaced by the relentless drum of the monsoon rain hammering the rusted corrugated roofs of the shipyard.

Chen slumped onto the maintenance grating, his chest heaving. "The beam," he choked out, wiping stinging salt from his eyes. "The Alpine link. It’s completely dead. We lost the carriage lock."

Lin pulled herself up, ignoring the hot trickle of blood running from her hairline down into her left eyebrow. She checked the optical transceiver’s azimuth ring. The heavy brass gimbal was warped three millimeters out of true where the sheared pins had buckled the deck plates.

Before she could reach for the alignment wrench, the yard’s open-channel maritime receiver began to squawk. The audio did not come through the encrypted mesh; it blasted over the international VHF distress frequency, cold, sterile, and perfectly synthesized.

"Attention all vessels in the Singapore and Malacca Straits Traffic Separation Scheme. By decree of the Admiralty Division and Euro-Asian Maritime Finance, the facility designated Keppel-Batam Drydock Four is declared an abandoned maritime hazard and an illegal salvage operation. All hull identification transfers, cargo clearances, and auxiliary power off-takes originating from this coordinate are nullified under international maritime lien. Vessels attempting to berth or discharge cargo will be deemed co-conspirators in salvage theft and subject to immediate impoundment."

Chen stared at the speaker. "Salvage theft? They financed those docks thirty years ago. They were written off as scrap after the second harbor subsidence!"

"They don't care about the scrap," Lin said, her voice stripped of inflection. She wiped her forehead with the sleeve of her grease-stained jacket. "They care about the precedent. If an unbonded crew can bring a dead yard back onto the ledger without their debt covenants, their whole risk-pricing model collapses."

Jin Wei’s heavy boots rang out on the iron ladder below. He hauled himself up to the lower platform, chewing methodically on a scrap of dried bitter melon rind—a somatic defense against the sulfur vapor that perpetually burned his lungs. In his hand, he held a carbon-copy clipboard scribbled with pencil marks.

"Two of the grain freighters from the Mekong delta just altered course," Jin said without greeting. "They picked up the admiralty warning. Their captains are refusing to drop anchor in our basin. They’re turning back toward the commercial roads. If they don't discharge their rice into our grain elevators by morning, their crews won't get paid, and the settlement at Berth Nine runs out of meal in three days."

"What about our battery reserves?" Lin asked, leaning against the crane cab to steady her trembling knees.

"Down to twenty-two percent," Jin replied grimly. "The tidal turbine in the south channel took a submerged drift log twenty minutes ago. The sheer-pin broke on the rotor hub. We're running purely on the tugboat packs, and the reverse-osmosis pumps are drinking four hundred amps just to keep fresh water flowing to the clinic."

They were being starved out in real time. Not by shells or torpedoes, but by the quiet, mathematical closure of maritime clearing accounts.

Lin looked past the dripping steel girders toward the south. Geneva was obscured by five hundred miles of storm front and severed glass lines across the Indian Ocean basin. But the Pacific horizon was different.

"We don't route through Europe," Lin said suddenly.

Chen frowned. "What are you talking about? The validation relay is in the Alps. The whole clearing tree—"

"The clearing tree is a distributed mesh, not a cathedral," Lin interrupted, her mind racing past the throbbing ache behind her temples. "Who holds the bulk of the unrefined energy buffer in the southern hemisphere right now? It isn't the North Atlantic banks."

Chen’s eyes widened. "The Andean mineral syndicate. The lithium salt nodes in the Atacama."

"They’re choked on dry inventory," Lin said, pulling the laser transceiver yoke toward her chest. Her shoulder muscles burned with exhaustion. "The regional haulage syndicates locked their railheads two weeks ago because the sovereign clearinghouse refused to settle their fuel vouchers. They have forty thousand tons of refined battery-grade carbonate sitting in rail spurs under the desert sun, completely immobilized because they lack spare parts and desalinated process water for their refining loops."

"And we have three million gallons of fresh water sitting in the deep ballast tanks," Jin murmured, his eyes narrowing. "And twelve empty bulk drydocks with heavy machine lathes."

"It’s an unbonded bilateral swap," Lin said, her fingers already working the vernier dials on the transceiver's manual pedestal. "Usufruct exchange. We grant them repair slots and desalinated water certificates for their trans-Pacific bulk carriers; they assign direct title to two thousand tons of dry-cell lithium salt to the Batam regional commons. No commercial banks. No clearinghouses. No maritime mortgage liens."

"Lin, the beam path to the Pacific transponder tower is over nine miles across open water," Chen warned, checking the handheld optical power meter. "The humidity is ninety-eight percent. The fog from the monitors hasn't even cleared. You’ll get sixty percent scatter on the cyan spectrum. The packet loss will tear the transaction blocks to pieces."

"Then we tune it by hand," Lin said.

She bent over the eyepiece. There was no automated tracking; the servos had burned out when the gantry shifted. Lin rested her cheek against the cold, damp iron of the mounting bracket. She remembered the nights during her apprenticeship, sitting in windowless transit stations, calculating coordinate vectors on greaseproof paper to pass the time. She knew the drift of this tower: two millimeters south on the ebb tide, half a millimeter east with every ten knots of westerly squall.

She sighted the faint, pulsing red navigation marker on the distant horizon of the Indonesian headland—the mountaintop relay tower that bypassed the coastal fiber choke points.

"Chen. Call out the signal-to-noise ratio. Don't look at the ledger. Look at the raw carrier wave."

"Carrier acquired," Chen muttered, his voice taut. "Attenuation... seventy-two percent. It’s too noisy, Lin. The checksum is failing."

"Compensating for wind sheer," Lin whispered. Her breath fogged the brass scale. She eased the manual micrometric screw a fraction of a thread. "Now."

"Forty-eight percent scatter. Packet reception... twenty percent. Thirty percent. It's fragmenting!"

From down on the quay, Uncle Tan’s voice crackled through the comm-box: "Jin! The south caisson valve is jamming! Silt in the gate guides! The dock is settling another degree to the port! If you don't lock that beam now, the tilt will take the transceiver completely off the horizon!"

"Lin!" Jin barked.

"Quiet," she breathed.

She didn't fight the crane's movement. Instead of trying to hold the crosshairs rigid against the storm, she anticipated the crane’s rhythmic, ponderous sway against the surging tide. She dialed the azimuth past the center mark, letting the structural flex of sixty tons of iron swing the beam directly through the receiver’s aperture at the crest of the swell.

A high, clean chime cut through the static on Chen’s handheld terminal.

"Handshake confirmed!" Chen yelled, his voice cracking. "The Atacama node answered! Cryptographic verification received... they’re validating the local sortition tally from yesterday’s assembly!"
