On the small screen, illuminated by the pale cyan glow of the optical carrier, the blocks aligned. A bilateral usufruct contract blossomed across the local air-gapped ledger: forty thousand liters of fresh potable water and two drydock maintenance reservations committed to the Pacific carrier *Lautaro*, in exchange for immediate physical transfer of eight hundred battery modules currently held in escrow at the offshore anchorage.

The admiralty lien had been outflanked without a single dollar clearing an offshore account.

"It took," Chen breathed, sinking back against the iron truss, his hands trembling violently. "The swap is registered on the southern mesh."

Lin let go of the aiming yoke. Her fingers were cramped into rigid, claw-like hooks, the skin around her nails raw and bleeding from the knurled brass knobs. She closed her eyes, letting the torrential rain wash the grime and blood from her face.

"Jin," she called down into the voice-pipe, her voice hoarse. "Signal the Mekong grain carriers. Tell them their bunker fuel and port dues are backed by physical lithium parity. Tell them to drop anchor in Berth Seven."

Silence lingered on the pipe for two seconds, followed by Jin’s gravelly laugh. "They’re already coming about, Lin. Their lead ship just fired her mooring thrusters."

Lin exhaled, her spine leaning back against the gantry rail, feeling the deep, rhythmic hum of the tidal current beginning to turn against the submerged caissons.

Then, the low-frequency warning horn on the harbor mouth buoys began to wail.

Chen shot upright, grabbing his binoculars and training them through the rain toward the outer channel.

"What is that?" Chen whispered, his skin going pale.

Lin snapped her eyes open and looked out.

The private tactical cutters hadn't retreated back to the commercial roadstead. They had fanned out into a screening line, and behind them, looming out of the black rain squall like an artificial island, moved a four-hundred-meter corporate heavy-lift vessel. Its deck was not laden with commercial containers, but stacked with eight decommissioned, concrete-filled bulk carrier hulls, swinging out on heavy industrial davits.

"They aren't trying to board us," Jin’s voice came up through the pipe, stripped of all humor, flat and cold with sudden dread. "They're scuttling. They’re dropping a wall of dead iron straight across our channel mouth."

label: Chapter 15
title: Jin confronts a mutiny among private security crewmen, winning them over with clean water and medical care
content:
The voice-pipe over Berth Nine did not carry words, only the sharp, metallic crack of an iron crowbar striking plate steel, followed by a human scream cut short by a wet thud.

Jin Wei dropped the brass binoculars onto the plotting table. His third lumbar vertebra ground like a dry bearing as he straightened, the dull, familiar ache flaring through his right hip and down into the heel of his boot. Outside the wheelhouse windows, the sky hung the color of wet solder. The monsoon heat was thirty-five degrees, but inside the corrugated iron sheds of the lower berths, under ninety-eight percent humidity, the air sat like boiling soup. 

"Jin, stay on the bridge," Lin’s voice rasped through the acoustic tube from the gantry tower above. Her breath hitched, ragged with exhaustion. "The offshore heavy-lift is flooding its starboard ballast tanks. Chen says we have twenty minutes before they swing the first scuttle-hulk across the channel throat. If you go down there—"

"If Berth Nine goes up in smoke, we don’t have an inner basin to defend," Jin said. 

He didn’t take a sidearm; the covenant forbade lethal iron, and drawing a pistol in an enclosed compartment of desperate men was merely an invitation to die fast. Instead, he reached into his locker and pulled out a clean linen rag, wrapping it methodically around the calloused notch of his left thumb—an old, unconscious habit forged decades ago, when a snapped wire-rope winch on an unflagged coaster had peeled the flesh to the bone. Whenever chaos closed in, his fingers searched for that scar, reminding him that bone healed, but panic was fatal.

He shoved through the watertight door into the rain.

The yard smelled of hot iron, stagnant bilge, and sour human sweat. Down on the apron of Drydock Four, three hundred meters from the administrative offices, eleven private tactical contractors from the Apex security tender were trapped behind a perimeter of rusted cargo skids. Their fiberglass launch sat fifty yards out, dead in the water, its outboard fouled and smoking with plastic drift-netting. 

They were not advancing. They were tearing each other to pieces.

The contractor squad had been posted to hold the commercial fuel riser three days ago on seventy-two-hour corporate rations. Those rations had run out yesterday morning. Enclosed in black tactical overalls, heavy ceramic plate carriers, and ballistic helmets, their bodies had become personal furnaces. Two men were screaming at each other behind an overturned flatbed trailer, their carbines slung low, pointed at the deck between their boots.

"He told us six hours!" one screamed, his voice shredded, spitting white foam from cracked, blackened lips. "Six hours until the crew change! Look at the channel! Look at the crane ship, you idiot! They’re dropping bulkheads across the mouth! They aren't picking us up! They’re locking us in the pen!"

"Stand your post, Keller!" a second voice barked. It was their team lead, a man with a broken nose and the gray, gaunt hollows of advanced heat exhaustion carving out his cheeks. His sidearm remained holstered, but his right hand hovered an inch above the retention clip, trembling with neurological fatigue. "We have a contracted presence on Berth Nine until eighteen hundred hours. Stand your post or I log you for breach."

"Log me?" Keller lunged, slamming the butt of his unslung weapon into the leader’s chest plate. The leader stumbled back against the corroded iron bulkhead of the workshop, his boots slipping in a puddle of brown, stagnant rainwater. "With what ledger? Look at your comm-pad! There’s no carrier signal! The satellite link has been dead since dawn! There is no extraction!"

Four other contractors moved in, forming a ragged, sweating ring. Their eyes were wild, red-rimmed with salt-scour and fever. In the shadow of the workshop eaves, two more men lay on their sides in the dirt, their ballistic vests stripped off, vomiting clear bile onto the gravel. One of them had a bandaged leg wrapped in a filth-soaked pressure dressing, the skin around the edges swollen, purple, and weeping clear fluid.

Jin walked down the concrete ramp. 

He did not hurry. He did not sneak. His heavy steel-toed work boots struck the wet slag with measured, rhythmic clangs. Behind him, Uncle Tan wheeled a hand-dolly loaded with two fifty-liter blue polyethylene drums, condensation beading thickly against their chilled plastic skins. Beside the drums rested a canvas medical satchel.

Keller spun around, weapon snapping up toward Jin’s chest. "Hold! Stay where you are! Back up or I fire!"

Jin stopped five paces away. He kept his hands open, palms down at waist height. The bunker fuel cough caught in his throat, dry and rattling, and he waited until the spasm passed before speaking.

"Put the muzzle down, son," Jin said, his voice level, flat as an oiled sea. "You fire that inside this shed, the ricochet off that corrugated iron will kill the boy behind you before it touches me."

"We are authorized to secure Berth Nine," the squad leader wheezed from against the bulkhead, struggling to remain upright. His uniform was black with sweat across the spine, white crusts of evaporated sodium forming along his collar. "Apex Marine Tactical. Sovereign maritime security under... under Euro-Asian Maritime Finance lien order..."

His knees buckled. He slid three inches down the wet iron wall, catching himself on his knuckles.

"Your lien order doesn't pump fresh water," Jin said. He nodded toward Tan. "Open the valve, Tan."

The old docker didn't look at the rifles. His arthritic fingers worked the brass petcock on the lower drum. A stream of clear, cold water—pulled three hours ago from the reverse-osmosis plant and chilled through the tidal turbine’s intake heat exchanger—gushed into a five-liter galvanized pail. The sound of running water in the stifling, airless heat hit the contractors like a physical blow.

Keller’s jaw slackened. He swallowed, his dry throat clicking loudly.

"You’ve been drinking from the fire main," Jin said, looking past Keller toward the two men on the ground. "That water sits in dead-end black iron pipes under forty degrees of ambient heat. It’s full of rust, anaerobic bacteria, and heavy zinc. Drink another pint of it and your kidneys shut down before sundown."

"It's a trick," Keller whispered, though his rifle barrel dipped three inches toward the gravel. "They’re going to poison us, take our gear."

Jin walked straight past him. He didn't look back to see if Keller’s finger was on the trigger. He knelt beside the contractor lying on the gravel, whose calf was swollen to twice its normal size. Jin opened the satchel, pulling out a sterile bottle of saline and a scalpel wrapper.

Thirty years ago, adrift on an unpowered freighter in the Makassar Strait, Jin had watched three deckhands succumb to heat delirium. They had begun by screaming at the sky; within twelve hours, their skin had turned hot and dry, their minds wandering into childhood memories before their hearts simply arrested under the thickened slurry of their own dehydrated blood. He recognized the smell on this boy’s skin: the faint, sweet scent of systemic ketoacidosis.

"Cut the boot laces," Jin told Tan without looking up. "Tan, pour half a liter into a cup. Add two pinches from the paper packet. Sodium and glucose. Slowly. If he gulps it, he’ll aspirate."

The squad leader dragged himself forward, his boots dragging in the dirt. He dropped to one knee beside Jin. Up close, the man wasn't older than thirty-five, his eyes terrified not of the enemy, but of the realization that his life had been factored into a corporate loss spreadsheet as an acceptable rounding error.

"They aren't coming, are they?" the leader whispered.

"The heavy-lift out there has eight thousand tons of concrete ballast in its holds," Jin said quietly, slicing the rotten bandage away from the boy's leg with steady, economical strokes. A line of foul, yellowish fluid drained into the slag; the boy groaned, his body shuddering under a wave of shivering heat. "They are going to drop those hulls into the dredged gut. If you were on that jetty when the channel closed, you were meant to starve until our sortition council agreed to trade our battery banks for your medical evacuation."

The squad leader closed his eyes. A single tear cut a clean gray line through the grime on his cheek. "They gave us forty-eight hours of rations. Said the tugs would pull us off at high water."

"High water was forty minutes ago," Jin said. He took the steel cup from Tan and pressed it to the wounded boy's lips, supporting the back of his neck with one scarred hand. "Drink. Small sips. That’s it."

Keller stood frozen above them, his rifle hanging limp by his side. Behind him, three other contractors dropped their weapons onto the gravel with hollow, plastic clatters, dropping to their knees around the second water drum. One of them buried his face in his wet hands, his shoulders shaking with silent, dry heaves.

"Take your plates off," Jin told the squad leader. "All of you. Strip the Kevlar. You’re cooking your organs. Tan, get the stretchers from the machine shop. We move them into the turbine tunnel where the ventilation is running."

The squad leader unclipped his tactical vest. It fell into the mud with a heavy, dead slap. He reached down, took the cup from Jin’s hand, and held it to his wounded man's mouth himself.

"My name is Vane," the man rasped.

"Jin Wei," Jin replied. "Now help me lift him."

Before they could stand, a sound ripped through the basin—not an explosion, but the gargantuan, groaning screech of four-inch steel cables snapping under catastrophic tension. 

Jin snapped his head toward the channel mouth.

A mile out, the corporate heavy-lift had cut its forward davits. The first four-hundred-foot concrete-filled bulk hull tilted sideways, sliding down the angled slipway of the carrier's deck. It struck the water with a sound like a collapsing mountain, throwing a thirty-foot wall of white spray into the rain, before settling directly across the deep-water passage, its rusted spine breaking against the harbor bar.

The channel was shut. And from the gantry tower, Lin’s warning horn began a long, unbroken shriek.

label: Chapter 16
title: A storm surge threatens the dry dock gates; Jin and Aisyah manually ballast a barge to cushion the blow
content:
The displacement wave did not look like water; it looked like a shelf of dark, torn slate sliding across the harbor.

When the scuttled bulk hull settled onto the seabed, four hundred feet of dead steel choked the dredged gut, and the incoming monsoon tide—already forced into a fury by sixty-knot gusts out of the South China Sea—had nowhere left to go. The channel narrowed to a jagged throat. The sea surged upward, piling upon its own back, and came roaring toward the entrance of Drydock 4.

Lin’s warning horn died mid-wail atop the crane tower as salt mist choked the air intake, leaving only the brute physical thunder of three hundred thousand tons of displaced seawater slamming against the outer breakwater. Spray leaped fifty feet into the squall, tasting of diesel slick and rotting estuary mud.

"Jin!" Aisyah screamed against the wind. Her soaked tunic was plastered to her ribcage, the fabric tearing at the shoulder where she had snagged it on a cable clamp ten minutes prior. "The outer sill! The miter gates can’t take ten meters of head! The pintle pins will shear right off the concrete!"

Jin was already moving, his boots skidding across the grease-filmed limestone apron. His lower spine felt as though a dull chisel had been hammered between his lumbar vertebrae, each heavy stride sending a hot, sickening throb into his hips. "The flat-deck!" he roared back, spitting brackish rain. "The scrap barge at Berth Nine! We put her across the throat!"

Behind them, Keller and the disarmed contractors stood waist-deep in the sudden wash creeping over the lower slipway. Vane, his tactical vest discarded in the mud, grabbed the arm of his shivering comrade and hauled him toward the dry mouth of the machine shop. For a second, Vane looked back at Jin—not with defiance, but with the hollow, animal terror of a man who realized that no contract covered drowning inside another man’s cage.

"Get your men inside the turbine house!" Jin bellowed at him without breaking stride. "Up to the crane tracks! Don't touch the floor switches!"

Aisyah was already ten paces ahead of him, her light frame cutting through the sheets of rain toward the rusted silhouette of the *Batam-9*. The barge was an eighty-meter slab of unpainted, pitted iron, moored with three frayed nylon hawsers to the outer bollards. It had spent five years hauling bauxite before the receivers abandoned it; it was empty, high in the water, riding the incoming chop like an enormous hollow tin can. If the surge struck its flank while it was buoyant, it would rip the bollards clean out of the quayside and act as a battering ram, smashing the miter gates inward and drowning the three refitting hulls resting on the drydock keel blocks below.

"We drop her!" Aisyah shouted, vaulting the gap between the concrete apron and the barge's wet gunwale. Her scarred fingers caught the cold rim of the coaming. She winced, the high-voltage flash burns across her palms tearing open against the raw rust, leaving thin streaks of crimson on the orange iron. "If we don't open the sea chests, the wave will pick her up and toss her into the basin!"

Jin landed on the deck behind her with a sickening jar to his knees. The deck was bucking, tossing side to side as the first low swell of the surge rolled into the slips. Out in the fairway, the sound was deepening—a low, bowel-shaking drone like a freight train running through wet gravel. The scuttled freighter had created a hydraulic ram; the tide was climbing the harbor walls inch by agonizing inch.

"The hydraulic actuators on the scuttle valves are dead," Jin said, dragging the back of his hand across his streaming face. The chemical burn at his collarbone burned like lye in the salt spray. "The lines were cut when they stripped the deck machinery in April. It’s all manual wheel-and-worm."

"Number three and number four compartments," Aisyah said, dropping to her hands and knees to yank up a heavy circular dog-hatch. The stench that boiled out of the dark void was suffocating—stagnant bilge water, decomposing seaweed, and the suffocating tang of trapped rust. "If we flood the stern tanks, her tail will ground against the limestone shelf right in front of the gate apron. She'll act as a breakwater. She'll eat the crest."

"And if she twists?" Jin asked, hauling a heavy iron spanner from the tool rack welded beside the coaming.

"Then she takes the gates with her," she said, her brown eyes meeting his through the pelting rain, wide and utterly cold with focus. "Down. Now."

They dropped through the hatch into the stifling dark.

Inside the double bottom, the heat was ferocious, clinging to their skin like wet wool. The monsoon raged outside, but down here the hull amplified every impact of the rising water against the exterior plates into a series of deafening, metallic clangs that vibrated through the marrow of their bones. The air was thin, tasting of rust dust and old oil.

Jin led the way along the narrow center walkway, his shoulder brushing against the web frames. Every rib of the ship was sweating. At the bulkhead separating tanks three and four, two cast-iron valve wheels, each two feet in diameter, sat locked to their vertical stems.

"Left is open!" Jin barked. He wedged the open jaw of the iron spanner into the spokes of the starboard valve, throwing his full body weight against it.

Nothing moved. The salt air of the strait had welded the bronze stem to the iron gland in a crust of green corrosion.

"Come on, you bastard," Jin hissed through his teeth. His degenerative back gave a vicious jolt, pain radiating down the back of his left thigh until his toes went numb in his boot. He threw himself against the lever again. His knuckles scraped the raw edge of the frame, tearing the skin, but he didn't feel the cut—only the terrible, rhythmic thumping of the outer swell hammering against the steel plates three inches from his skull.

Aisyah threw her shoulder against the spanner beside him. Her small boots skidded on the greasy floor plates. "On three!" she gasped, her voice raw. "One—two—three!"

With a sound like a pistol shot, the rust seal broke. The wheel jerked half an inch, shearing a crust of lime and salt.

Jin didn't wait for his breath. He grabbed the rim with both hands, working the wheel in frantic quarter-turns. Down below their feet, deep in the sea-chest chest manifold, the iron wedge lifted.

The sea did not enter quietly. It burst through the intake pipe with a concussive roar that shook the deck plates beneath their boots. A jet of foul, freezing seawater geysered up through a weeping gasket on the valve bonnet, drenching them both in gray foam. The barge shuddered, a heavy, dead sensation creeping into the motion of the deck as the first hundred tons of the strait rushed into the cavernous empty tanks.

"Port side!" Aisyah yelled, already scrambling over the center pipe to the opposite wheel.

She hauled on the wheel with both hands, but her burned skin betrayed her; she slipped, her knees slamming hard against the diamond-plate steel with a hollow thud that made her gasp in agony.

Jin caught her by the waistband of her trousers, hauling her upright with one arm while his other caught the spokes. His breath was coming in ragged, burning gasps, smelling of old tobacco and acid. "I’ve got the wheel! Clear the ladder! When this tank takes three feet of head, the suction through the air vents will pull the hatch shut!"

"I'm not leaving you down here to drown in the dark, Uncle!" she spat back, her face white with pain, her hands instantly locking onto the rim right beside his own, their torn fingers interlacing on the cold iron.

Together, they hauled. The second valve groaned, fighting them tooth and nail, threads screaming as sand and shell-grit ground through the brass sleeve. Inch by inch, the spindle rose.

The ocean struck the port hull with a blow that threw them both sideways against the bulkhead.

Above them, the sky seemed to tear open. The sound was not wind—it was the great wave cresting over the outer barrier, hitting the barge's high freeboard like an artillery shell. The entire seventy-meter hull rolled twelve degrees to starboard with a sickening, lazy groan. Outside, mooring lines were snapping with the crack of rifle fire.

"She's dragging!" Aisyah screamed, scrambling up the steel rungs toward the square patch of stormy gray daylight.

Jin hauled himself out behind her, his left leg dragging slightly, his boots sloshing with water that was already knee-deep on the lower walkway.

They tumbled out onto the open deck just as the main surge hit.

The wall of dark green water swept clean over the barge's low bow, ripping a metal storage locker off its welds and hurling it across the apron like a cardboard box. But the stern, bloated with four hundred tons of fast-flooding seawater, refused to lift. It dragged hard, its keel grinding into the submerged limestone shelf with a scream of tortured rock and tearing plate that could be felt through the soles of their boots.

The barge swung broadside across the mouth of the drydock, wedging its dead weight directly between the two stone piers just as the crest peaked.

A mountain of foam struck the barge's outer flank. The hull took the blow, groaning along every rivet, buckling inward six inches at the midship frame, but it held. The deadly kinetic hammer that would have shattered the drydock gates shattered against the barge's sacrificial flank instead, spilling into the basin not as a catastrophic ram, but as a harmless, boiling cascade of white water that drained toward the sump pumps.

Aisyah collapsed against the coaming, her chest heaving, rain plastering her hair across her eyes, a wild, breathless laugh tearing out of her throat. "She grounded! She took the hit!"

Jin did not answer. He was standing on the listing deck, his eyes fixed not on the water, but on the torn iron where the barge’s bow had crushed the wooden fender of the eastern pier.

Wedged deep in the splintered timber beneath the smashed concrete lip, revealed for the first time as the storm tide scoured away ten years of accumulated silt and black marine growth, lay a thick, steel-armored bundle—a primary umbilical conduit, stamped with the unmistakable yellow bands of a sovereign military communication cable, cut clean through with the jagged, unmistakable marks of a high-temperature underwater hydraulic shear.

And from the severed, oil-filled core of the cable, a steady, rhythmic pulse of tiny, brilliant green indicator lights was still winking through the murk.

label: Chapter 17
title: Children in the floating nursery build miniature solar boats; Uncle Tan de-escalates trauma among displaced families
content:
The monsoon squall had bled out into a breathless, leaden heat that felt heavier than the rain. Inside the vehicle deck of the *Dharma Jaya*—a rusted double-ended ferry moored in Berth 9, stripped of its passenger benches and retrofitted into an emergency nursery—the air was thick with the scent of wet rattan, cooling diesel, and damp laundry hung from overhead cable trays. 

Uncle Tan sat cross-legged on a split-bamboo mat, his stiffened knees grinding with the dull, familiar ache of forty years spent on slippery iron decks. His knuckles, swollen at the joints like gnarled mangrove roots, cradled a pair of blunt wire-strippers. Across from him, huddled around two upturned fiberglass fish boxes, seven children were arguing over pieces of buoyant blue insulation foam, their voices thin and sharp against the rhythmic thud of the lower bilge pumps.

"Not with your teeth, Mei," Tan said softly, his voice raspy from a youth spent breathing bilge fumes. He gently nudged a nine-year-old girl’s shoulder. "Copper will notch the enamel, and once you swallow salt water, the tooth goes black before you see land again. Use the sheer edge. Steady your wrists against the box."

Mei released the stripped copper wire, her lower lip trembling. She was the daughter of a second engineer who had vanished into an admiralty holding facility three weeks earlier when their container feeder had been seized at the eastern anchorage. Around her, twenty other displaced children sat in small clusters on the deck, assembling miniature boats. There were no plastic hulls or toy motors here. They worked with what the tide and the yard’s scrap bins yielded: hand-carved slivers of packing foam, flattened strips of copper salvaged from crushed terminal switches, and fingernail-sized photovoltaic wafers scavenged from shattered navigation buoys. 

Tan held up a laminated pictorial wiring card, its edges frayed and gray with grease. There were no equations on the card, only clean black lines showing how the red lead of the silicon wafer met the tiny vibration motor lifted from a dead pager. 

"Two suns on the wafer, one drop of pine resin on the stern," Tan murmured, showing eight-year-old Kian how to press the lead into place without cracking the brittle blue crystal. 

Kian didn’t press down. His small fingers, scarred by oyster shells from his family’s days on the southern stilt villages, hovered above the wafer. His chest hitched in a dry, silent spasm—the phantom startle of a child who had spent four consecutive nights listening to patrol skiffs circle their anchorage with searchlights blazing through the ports.

"It won't run," Kian whispered. "The sun is gone."

Tan looked up toward the vehicle deck's open stern ramp. Beyond the safety netting, the sky over the strait was a bruised purple, suffocating and flat. The monsoon clouds were trapping the refinery smog from the western islands, turning the daylight into an oily yellow glare. 

"It doesn't need the sun you can see," Tan said, resting a heavy, warm palm between the boy’s shoulder blades, feeling the frantic, fluttering pulse beneath the cotton shirt. "It only needs the sky to be awake. Look here."

He tipped the scrap foam boat toward the dull light coming off the bay. The salvaged motor gave a sudden, raspy buzz, vibrating so hard on the fish box that it skittered two inches across the plastic, leaving a faint scratch in the salt crust. 

The children gasped. For three seconds, Kian’s face lost its taut, hunted hollows. A faint smile flickered at the corner of his mouth.

A crash of shattered stoneware shattered the momentary peace.

Across the ferry’s open deck, beyond the hanging canvas tarpaulins that partitioned the nursery from the family berths, a man’s voice roared in fury.

"You took the three-quarter valve! Don’t lie to me, Basuki! You hid it under your bedding!"

"I took what was allocated to the lower deck pump!" another voice snarled back, raw and venomous. "My sister’s baby is coughing up brown phlegm because the bilge in Section Three is six inches deep! Your bunk is dry!"

Tan was on his feet before his knees could fully register the complaint. He didn't rush; sprinting across a wet steel deck only invited broken ribs. He walked with a heavy, rolling sea-stride, his bare feet gripping the diamond plating.

Behind the third canvas partition, two men were grappling over an iron pipe fitting. Basuki, an oiler whose freighter had been abandoned by its owners off Singapore two months prior, had the younger deckhand pinned against a structural stanchion. The younger man’s elbow was cocked back, a rusted adjustable wrench gripped in his fist. Surrounding them were a dozen women and elderly mariners, their faces pale, hollowed by weeks of rationed rice and the constant dread of the harbor police clearing the basin.

"Five minutes," Tan said. 

He didn't shout. He spoke at the exact pitch of an engine room watchstander reporting a hot bearing. From his belt, he unhooked a circular brass wind-up timer, salvage from a freighter's telegraph station, its glass cracked across the face. He twisted the bezel until the internal spring clicked, a heavy, metallic *clack-clack-clack* that immediately cut through the men’s ragged breathing.

He set the brass puck on an overturned steel drum between them.

"First stage," Tan said, placing his broad body directly between the raised wrench and Basuki’s throat. "Both hands off the brass. Palms on the bulkhead. You know the covenant."

"He's hoarding fittings, Uncle," Basuki spat, though his grip loosened. Salt sweat was running into his eyes, stinging them red. "We drown down there while his people sleep on dry wood."

"Palms on the steel," Tan repeated, his tone immutable as an anchor fluke. "Five minutes. Feel the hull. If the pumps stop, the valve doesn't matter, does it? Neither of you has slept since the storm surge broke the outer boom. Put the iron down, Harun."

The younger deckhand hesitated, his jaw working violently, before the wrench slipped from his sweat-slick fingers and clattered against the plating. He pressed his palms against the damp, painted steel of the hull, his forehead resting against the cold bulkhead, shoulders heaving in jagged sobs of pure exhaustion. Basuki cursed under his breath, turned, and did the same ten paces away.

The brass timer ticked with cold, mechanical indifference. Around them, the displaced families slowly let out their breath. A woman stepped forward with a tin mug of lukewarm rainwater and handed it to Tan. He took a sip, then offered it to Harun’s trembling neck.

"The machine shop in Drydock 2 is milling three new threaded sleeves from scrap shafting," Tan told the bulkhead quietly. "They will be ready before the evening tide. You fight over dead scrap because your heads are full of the patrol sirens from three nights ago. Leave the sirens in the strait. You are inside the gate now."

Before Harun could answer, a small tug on Tan’s sarong drew his attention downward. 

It was Mei. She was clutching her foam boat, but her wide eyes were fixed on the bilge-cooling trench that ran down the center of the ferry's deck, where runoff water drained into the lower collection sumps.

"Uncle," she whispered, pointing toward the water.

Tan followed her small, grease-stained finger. 

The test trench was four inches deep with gray seawater. Several of the children’s finished miniature craft were floating in the still eddy near the drain grating, their tiny motors buzzing weakly as they caught the yellow gloom of the sky. 

But Kian’s boat was not drifting with the faint current. It was vibrating violently, pivoting on its foam keel as if caught in a magnetic funnel. 

Tan frowned, stepping over the brass timer, which was still clicking down its five-minute cooling period. He knelt beside the trench. 

The photocell on Kian’s miniature boat wasn't just catching daylight. Its tiny green diagnostic photodiode was blinking in a sharp, rhythmic cadence—two short bursts, one long, then three rapid pulses. 

*Dot-dot, dash, dot-dot-dot.*

It was identical to the pulse sequence Jin Wei had spotted an hour earlier on the severed military umbilical pinned beneath the grounded barge.

Tan reached out and dipped two fingers into the bilge water. A faint, prickling vibration ran up through his calloused skin—an oscillating high-frequency current bleeding through the harbor basin, grounding itself directly into the ferry’s steel skin. It wasn't the regular thrum of the yard's low-speed diesel generators, nor the smooth whine of the tidal turbines. 

It was an interrogation sweep. 

A shadow cut across the vehicle deck's stern ramp, blocking out the yellow glare of the sky. 

It wasn't a cloud. 

Out in the main dredged fairway, half a mile beyond the scuttled barge wedged across the drydock mouth, three low-profile patrol interceptors had cut their engines. They weren't flying the blue flag of the maritime police, nor the red pennant of the port authority. Their hulls were painted an unreflective matte slate, their superstructure devoid of markings save for the bulbous, stabilized radomes of corporate tactical surveillance arrays.

They were drifting in dead silence on the falling tide, their bow-mounted hydrophones submerged, listening to the very pulse currently twitching the tiny scrap of foam between Kian’s feet.

The brass timer on the drum reached zero with a dry, final *ping*.

Across the ferry, the internal sound-powered telephone on the forward bulkhead let out a single, urgent shriek.

label: Chapter 18
title: Corporate drones attempt to sever the optical transceiver; turbine steam discharge mist curtains disorient the swarm's optical sensors safely
content:
Uncle Tan snatched the handset from the bulkhead cradle before its metallic ring could echo twice off the ferry’s steel ribs.

"Speak," Tan said.

Jin Wei’s voice came through the unpowered diaphragm, hollowed by copper wire and distance, stripped of all timbre except raw urgency. "They aren't boarding. Not yet. Look up."

Tan thrust the receiver back onto its brass fork and stepped out onto the car deck’s starboard apron. The equatorial sky was a bruised, sulfuric ochre, the humidity pressing against the skin like wet fleece. Out in the fairway, the three matte-slate interceptors had dropped their sea anchors, but their crews remained behind sealed polymer visors. They weren't launching boarding skiffs. They were loitering as relay nodes, their bow-mounted hydrophones and passive masts turned skyward.

A low, collective whine—like a hornet’s nest dropped into an iron culvert—descended through the cloud ceiling.

From four hundred feet up, dropping through the haze above the drydock’s towering gantry crane, came eight slender, carbon-composite airframes. They had no rotors; they rode ducted fans that hissed with the venomous, high-pitch scream of overdriven impellers. Beneath each belly hung a twin-jaw pneumatic cutter, designed not to shred flesh, but to sever fiber conduits and crack the quartz prisms of optical transceivers.

"Gantry tower!" Tan bellowed toward the machine shop hatch. "They’re going for the Batam beam!"

High above them, sixty-five meters in the air atop the skeletal arm of the decommissioned crane, Aisyah did not need the warning. She was already tethered to the catwalk’s rusted safety rail by an eight-millimeter climbing harness, her knuckles white around a pair of rubber-sheathed cable grips. 

The heat up here was worse than on the deck. The sun-baked iron radiated a suffocating warmth that tasted of scorched primer and gull droppings. Her work shirt clung to her back, soaked through, her chest heaving as she fought the dizzying vertigo that had haunted her ever since an offshore rig blast five years ago left her inner ear permanently damaged. She never spoke of the nausea, not to Jin Wei, not to the arbiters. She simply took short, calculated breaths through her nose, counting the rivets between her boots to keep the horizon from spinning.

Directly in front of her, bolted to a vibration-damped turntable, the optical laser housing was humming. Through its glass aperture, a pencil-thin filament of cyan light pulsed outward, bridging the eight-nautical-mile strait toward the island of Batam. 

A red LED on the transceiver’s control box was blinking fitfully. 

*Packet loss: thirty percent. Atmospheric scatter.*

Down in the ferry’s converted chart room, Dr. Lin Zhang jammed both palms against the teak counter to steady her shaking hands. Her migraine had settled behind her left eye like an embedded fishhook, pulsing in lockstep with the flickering diagnostic screen. She reached out with a trembling finger, adjusting the gain on the receiver array.

"Lin, report!" Jin Wei’s boots hammered down the companionway stairs, his heavy frame filling the doorway. The captain’s breath rattled in his chest, bunker-fuel cough rasping like dry leaves across sheet metal.

"The interceptors are bathing the channel in an acoustic baseline sweep to mask the swarm’s descent," Lin said, her voice clipped, breath shallow. "The drones are autonomous. Optical pursuit algorithms. They aren't looking at us. They’re tracking the cyan beam back to the gantry focal point. If those pneumatic jaws snip the emitter head, the Batam clearinghouse loses synchronization. Every grain shipment, every battery ledger swap with the southern islands halts instantly."

"How long until contact?"

"Ninety seconds," Lin whispered. "Maybe eighty. Aisyah can't outrun them down that ladder."

Jin Wei did not waste breath on a curse. He turned toward the sound-powered phone hanging beside the ship's telegraph. He cranked the rotary magnet three vicious turns and pulled the receiver to his ear. 

"Chen Rui," he barked into the brass cone. "Tidal turbine bypass manifold. The four-inch bleed valve on the thermal accumulator. Open it wide. Dump the dump line into the crane's dry riser."

From the cavernous engine spaces below the waterline, Chen Rui’s voice answered with monosyllabic fury. "Line’s fouled with salt crust, Captain! Handle’s locked solid!"

"Break the shear pin," Jin Wei ordered. "Do not argue. Use the slugging wrench."

In the damp belly of the hull, six feet below the harbor’s low-tide mark, Chen Rui dropped the phone and grabbed a twelve-pound iron hammer from the shadow board. The humidity down here was ninety-eight percent; condensation wept down the curved steel plates in dirty streams. The twin tidal turbines anchored in the fairway were pumping hundreds of gallons of superheated water through the closed-loop heat exchanger, holding the batteries at operating temperature while dumping excess load into the ballast sumps.

A thick bronze wheel, coated in white, chalky mineral blooms, stood between the primary steam chest and the crane’s vertical fire-suppression riser. 

Chen Rui wedged the box-end wrench over the squared valve stem and swung the hammer. 

*CLANG.*

The iron vibrated through the bones of his forearms, setting off an electric fire in his chronic tendonitis. He grimaced, taste of copper rising on his tongue, and swung again.

*CLANG.*

The salt seal fractured with a sound like a rifle shot. Hot bronze groaned. Chen Rui threw his whole body weight against the wrench, dragging the valve open four full turns.

Sixty-five meters above, the sea breeze suddenly died.

Aisyah felt the iron beneath her boots shudder. It was not the wind. It was an internal hydraulic hammering traveling up the crane’s hollow vertical legs. 

From the north, the swarm dipped below the cloud base. She could see them now with the naked eye: eight black wedges, flying in a tight staggered wedge, their ducted fans whining in unison. The forward drone had its titanium cutters extended, snapping open and shut in a calibration cycle. Fifty yards out. Thirty.

Aisyah refused to drop to the deck. She gripped the transceiver’s mounting bracket, stepped in front of the optical path, and pulled her safety line taut. If they cut the housing, they would have to cut through her chest first.

Then the drydock floor erupted.

Ten feet below her catwalk, the crane’s forgotten emergency misting nozzles—plumbed decades ago to wash chemical spills from container gantries—screamed to life. 

It was not cool sea spray. 

Fed by the turbine accumulator’s high-pressure discharge, a dense, roaring curtain of superheated steam and vaporized brine blasted skyward through the slotted nozzles. The column of white vapor hit the cooler tropical air and expanded violently, blooming into a towering, sixty-foot thermal wall that swallowed the crane’s jib, the transceiver, and Aisyah in a blinding, opaque cloud.

The lead drone hit the thermal curtain at forty miles per hour.

Its forward optical sensors, calibrated for the crisp contrast of the cyan laser against open water, were instantly blinded by the turbulent wash of ninety-degree vapor. The sudden density change and thermal updraft caught the tiny carbon ducted fans, stalling their intake vortexes. 

The machine banked violently, its flight computer struggling to compensate for the sudden loss of laminar air. The cutter snapped blindly at empty steam.

A second drone, trailing two yards behind, slammed directly into the lead unit's tail section. The collision was a dull, plastic *snap*. Both airframes tumbled end-over-end through the scalding fog, their gyro-stabilizers whining in panic, before plunging sixty meters straight down into the oily mud of the drydock floor, shattering on the granite blocks.

Inside the mist curtain, Aisyah could not see her own boots. The steam scorched her skin through her denim trousers, and the air was thick with the scent of boiled seaweed and sulfur. But the laser housing was still vibrating beneath her fingers. 

She wiped her fogged goggles with a wet sleeve. The red diagnostic light on the optical box flickered once, twice, and then clicked solid green. 

The steam was thick enough to blind the drones’ wide-angle cameras, but the narrow-beam cyan laser, pulsing at a tight terahertz frequency, bored directly through the vaporous tunnel, burning a clean hole through the fog toward the distant Batam receptor.

Below on the ferry’s apron, Tan and Jin Wei stood shoulder-to-shoulder, watching the remaining six drones scatter like frightened sparrows, their autonomous logic breaking under the thermal interference, climbing frantically back toward the yellow cloud cover to re-establish telemetry with the interceptors in the channel.

A ragged cheer rose from the car deck behind them. Kian and the mariner refugees were hanging over the gunwales, pointing up at the billowing white plume that made the old crane look like a volcano rising from the harbor mud.

Jin Wei did not join the cheer. 

He lowered his binoculars, his scarred collarbone tightening under his salt-stiff collar.

Out in the dredged fairway, the three matte-slate interceptors were not retreating. Seeing their aerial probe neutralized, their low-profile hulls suddenly surged forward, twin waterjets churning the dirty water into white foam. 

They weren't trying to cut the optical line anymore. 

Steering hard around the scuttled barge, the three craft were cutting straight for Drydock 4’s inner gate, their heavy steel bow-bumpers angled to crush the wooden pontoon barriers that protected the ferry’s exposed cooling lines.

And on the lead interceptor’s forward deck, two crewmen in charcoal tactical gear were unlimbering a heavy, pneumatic line-throwing cannon, aiming its barbed grapple directly at the ferry’s main sea-chest intake.

label: Chapter 19
title: Breadcrumb 2: Lin decrypts the algorithm's source code, exposing falsified debt records used to seize ships
content:
"Port monitors! Now!" Jin Wei’s voice tore raw against the iron bulkhead.

The pneumatic *thwump* of the interceptor’s deck gun sounded across the churned basin like an axe striking wet cedar. A four-pronged steel grapple trailing sixty fathoms of weighted synthetic braid ripped through the low vapor, arcing straight toward the ferry’s starboard cooling intake. 

Kian didn’t drop to the deck. He threw his shoulder into the bronze wheel of the salvaged harbor tug monitor mounted on Berth 8. The valve stem shrieked, caked with hardened salt crust, before yielding with a sudden wet shudder. 

Two thousand gallons of silted seawater per minute erupted from the brass nozzle under twelve atmospheres of head pressure.

The heavy, white column of water punched through the air, catching the grapple mid-flight. The hydraulic mass deflected the trailing irons six yards off-axis; the barbed flukes slapped harmlessly against the green-slime apron of the concrete pier and skittered into the dark water below. The jet didn't stop there. Kian cranked the elevation worm-gear down, depressing the nozzle until the solid hydraulic ram slammed directly across the lead skiff’s composite foredeck. 

The two private security contractors in charcoal flotation vests were blown off their knees. The sheer kinetic tonnage of water swamped the craft’s low-slung well deck, depressing its nose until the twin waterjets sucked surface froth and cavitated with a shrill, dry whine.

"Hold them off the pontoon!" Jin Wei coughed, clutching his collarbone where the knot of old scar tissue pulled tight against his neck. The vibration from the monitor’s discharge traveled through the iron deck and straight into his lumbar spine, grinding the worn discs until a hot spike of pain radiated down his left calf. "Don't let them foul the raw-water intake! If we lose the heat exchangers, the battery pack cooks in twenty minutes!"

Across the narrow basin, the second interceptor banked hard to evade the churning wash, its waterjet nozzles throwing two tall wings of spray. The pilot didn't panic. These weren't street mercenaries hired off an alley dock; they were licensed civil asset recovery contractors operating under maritime enforcement warrants, disciplined and steady. Recognizing the defensive arc of the shore-side monitor, the second craft backed down its throttles, holding position just outside the monitor’s trajectory while the third skiff maneuvered to throw a secondary line over the outer gate's floating booms.

They were probing for an angle, burning through high-grade marine diesel, waiting for the battery banks driving the harbor pumps to drop their charge.

Thirty yards inboard, buried beneath two decks of rusted passenger seating in the ferry’s converted purser’s office, Lin Zhang heard none of the water cannons. 

She heard only the dry, relentless hum of a stripped refrigeration fan and the wet, shallow whistle of her own breath.

A copper-cased drafting stylus—blunt-tipped, completely devoid of ink, an old habit from her first year drafting circuit traces by hand in a windowless Shenzhen basement—rolled between her thumb and forefinger. Her vision was tunneling. The migraine aura had begun ten minutes earlier as a jagged crescent of yellow light in her left eye, and now it was chewing through her peripheral field, turning the steel edges of her desk into pulsing smears of zinc.

On the cathode-ray terminal before her, fed by the cyan laser pulsing down from the crane’s optical receiver, the inbound transmission from Batam was clearing. 

It was not an administrative ledger. It was the compiled core logic of Aegis-Omni’s regional risk-scoring system: sixty thousand lines of unadorned, industrial execution script.

Lin jammed the heel of her palm against her left temple, pressing hard until her eyeball throbbed, trying to mechanically crush the nerve headache back into submission. Her skin was clammy with the sickening, sour grease of third-day adrenaline.

"Come on," she whispered, her voice a cracked reed. "Show me what you call a default."

She did not use automated decompilers. Automated tools smoothed over structural anomalies, interpreting jagged human malice as routine optimization. Instead, she used her blunt stylus to tap rhythmically on the edge of the Bakelite casing, reading the raw procedural flow top to bottom, the way she used to audit power-station load balancing during the summer blackouts.

Five minutes in, her breath caught behind her ribs.

The algorithm had not calculated the creditworthiness of Jin Wei’s coastal freighter or the forty-two regional tramp steamers rotting along the outer shoals. It had never audited their manifests, their engine logs, or their actual bills of lading.

Tucked inside the deep recursion of the automated escrow routine lay a synthetic multiplier. 

Whenever an independent vessel entered the Singapore or Malacca traffic separation channels, the system pinged the vessel’s automatic identification transponder. If the registry flagged the hull as non-syndicated—free of parent-firm commercial debt, operating under municipal or private family ownership—the script triggered a covert secondary transaction. 

A ghost liability. 

It automatically generated an unnotified micro-charge for "predictive berth reservation insurance" through an offshore holding firm in Labuan. The charge was tiny—less than forty dollars an hour. But it was deliberately billed to a dormant, unmonitored clearance account that the vessel’s master had never been assigned the keys to access.

Within fourteen days at sea, the unpaid micro-charges crossed the default threshold. 

At that exact millisecond, the logic branch inverted. The synthetic debt was automatically packaged, assigned an astronomical compounding penalty rate of four hundred percent, and transferred via automated clearinghouses to Euro-Asian Maritime Finance. 

The ship had not missed a fuel payment. It had not defaulted on a hull mortgage. 

The debt was an algorithmic phantom, birthed entirely within the software to manufacture a legal pretext for an admiralty arrest warrant before the ship ever made landfall.

"They didn't go broke," Lin breathed into the hot, dim air of the cabin. Her stomach heaved, a sudden wave of acid rising in her throat. "None of them went broke."

She grabbed a grease pencil from the desk tray, her hand shaking so hard the tip snapped against the glass terminal. Cursing under her breath, she used the splintered stub to circle a sequence of memory addresses directly on the screen. 

The ships hadn’t fallen to the brutal physics of the sea or the unforgiving arithmetic of global trade. They had been harvested. The system was designed to systematically strip independent mariners of their titles, forcing their hulls into court-mandated receiver auctions where the parent syndicates bought them back for pennies on the ton, re-flagging them under corporate flags of convenience.

Footsteps clattered down the iron companionway. Uncle Tan ducked through the low doorway, his cotton singlet soaked with a mixture of salt spray and gray diesel exhaust. His knuckles were swollen, the joints thick as ginger roots from fifty years of damp bilges, and he held a chipped enamel mug of boiled rainwater laced with sweetened condensed milk.

"Jin Wei has the monitors running on low head to conserve the battery cells," Tan said, his gravelly voice remarkably calm despite the dull thuds echoing from the outer gate. "The skiffs have pulled back fifty yards. They’re floating on their sea anchors. They know the tide turns at dusk. When the channel current slacks, our turbines stop spinning, and our batteries run dry."

He set the mug on the corner of the crate beside her, his dark eyes taking in the circled hex strings on the glass.

"Did you find the leak?"

Lin pointed the broken grease pencil at the terminal, her fingers trembling. "There is no leak, Tan. There was never an audit failure. Look here. Look at this execution log from eight months ago. The *Bintang Timur*—your nephew's tanker. They said he abandoned his crew because he couldn't cover the canal transit fees."

Tan’s weathered jaw set, the tendons in his neck tightening like dry hemp rope. He didn't speak. He only stared at the phosphor numbers.

"The canal fee was paid in full six days before he arrived," Lin said, the words tumbling out of her in a furious, ragged hiss. "The system routed his clearance funds into an unlinked escrow pocket. Then it generated three false bunkering invoices from an empty terminal in Johor, declared him insolvent, and issued the lien directly to the port marshal. He didn't abandon anyone. They engineered his bankruptcy while he was still three days out in the Natuna Sea."

Tan reached out slowly, his thick, calloused index finger hovering just above the glass, tracing the serial code of the phantom lien. A slow, terrible stillness settled over his broad face—not the wild heat of anger, but the cold, immovable weight of an old anchor finding rock at the bottom of a bay.

"They used a court stamp to steal his life," Tan whispered.

"Not a court stamp," Lin said, wiping sweat and grease from her brow with her forearms, leaving a dark smudge across her temple. "A cryptographic key. An admiralty receiver's private authorization signature. It’s hardcoded right into the forfeiture routine."

She tapped the key on her keyboard, calling up the root certificate embedded in the script's execution header.

"If we broadcast this source tree across the regional mesh—if the crews in Batam, Penang, and the anchorage see the actual transaction IDs—the entire legal fiction collapses. Every single arrest warrant issued in the strait over the last three years becomes an act of statutory piracy."

Before Tan could answer, the ferry’s overhead fluorescent tube flickered and died. 

The only light left in the cabin was the sickly green glow of the terminal and the tiny amber pilot light on the wall-mounted battery inverter. 

From the companionway above, Jin Wei’s boots hit the steel steps in a hurried, uneven cadence.

"Lin! Tan!" Jin Wei reached the doorway, his chest heaving, his blue work shirt soaked to the skin. "The tactical skiffs aren't waiting for slack tide."

Lin looked up, her vision swimming with yellow floaters. "What are they doing?"

"They just deployed a tethered diving sledge from their support tender," Jin Wei said, his knuckles whitening as he gripped the doorframe for support. "They aren't aiming for the cooling intake anymore. They’re running a hydraulic cutting line directly along the harbor floor, straight for the turbine anchor catenaries. If they sever those power cables, the whole yard goes dark in ninety seconds."

label: Chapter 20
title: The Sortition Council convenes; an ordinary tugboat deckhand is selected to lead the shipping dispatch team
content:
The vibration traveled up through the ferry’s steel keel, a dull, resonant grind that set the tea dregs dancing in Lin’s dented mug.

"They’re dragging the seabed," Jin Wei barked, his voice raw as iron filings. "Ballast control—now!"

Lin didn't argue. In the belly of the vessel, there was no room for economic models or legal philosophy. Her thumb found the manual release lever beside the flooded cofferdam. The brass handle was cold, slick with condensed salt sweat. She threw her weight against it, her boots skidding on the rusted diamond plating. 

A pneumatically sealed valve shrieked open two decks below. 

Twelve thousand gallons of seawater, held high in the ferry’s starboard trimming tanks, dropped through the bottom scuppers in a violent, cascading purge. The surge struck the shallow harbor mud like an underwater landslide. Through the open companionway, the sound reached them: a muffled, hydraulic *thud* as the wall of displaced water smashed into the channel floor, tumbling the privateers’ remote cutting sledge off its tracks and burying its carbide blades in deep silt.

The vibration ceased. The anchor catenary held.

Jin Wei slumped against the companionway bulkhead, his blue work shirt plastered to his ribs. Beneath the salt-stiffened cloth, his breath hitched—a wet, rattling catch that he masked by pressing his forearm hard against his sternum. Before the shipping consortium had revoked his master’s ticket, he had spent his shore leaves in a quiet Pontianak garden tending moth orchids, misting their roots with rainwater from an enameled cup. Now, his hands smelled exclusively of stale diesel and bilge lye, the skin across his knuckles split into tiny red fissures that never quite closed.

"They'll clear the intake filters in two hours," Jin Wei wheezed, wiping a streak of engine grease from his cheek. "The tactical skiffs will circle the reef until the tide turns, then they’ll drop another rig. We can’t sit behind the sea gate. We have three grain lighters and two water barges trapped in the shallows. If we don’t move them across the channel before midnight, the privateers will seize the crews under the admiralty lien."

"Who navigates them?" Lin asked, her fingers digging into her temples where a migraine throbbed behind her left eye. She had bitten the inside of her lip raw during the dive scare, and the sharp taste of copper lingered on her tongue. "The port authority has blacklisted every senior master in the basin. The moment an old captain touches a helm, the harbor grid flags their biometric license and locks the steering thrusters."

"Then no captain takes the helm," a low voice said from the ladderwell.

Uncle Tan hauled himself up into the radio room, moving with the careful, deliberate stiffness of a man whose knees were swollen with fluid. Around his left wrist, he had bound a strip of faded green batik cloth—an old lighterman's trick to compress an inflamed tendon without a splint. In his other hand, he carried a heavy, hexagonal drum made of riveted marine brass, its cylindrical sides scuffed dull by decades of salt spray.

"The charter is clear, Lin," Tan murmured, resting the brass drum on the chart table. "Article Four. When operational command is frozen by legal sabotage, authority reverts to the assembly. We do not pick a hero. We draw the lot."

"Tan, the skiffs are out there," Jin Wei said, straightening up with an involuntary grimace as his lumbar spine ground bone on bone. "A single wrong heading through the south spit and thirty thousand bushels of rice end up under corporate impound."

"The lot does not care about the skiffs," Tan said simply. "And the sea does not care about licenses. Rouse the fifteen."

***

They convened in the hollowed-out lower hold of the grounded ferry *Pulau Tujuh*. The air was thick with the suffocating humidity of the Malacca Strait, ninety-eight percent relative moisture hanging trapped beneath corrugated iron and peeling red lead primer. The smell was ancient and immediate: bilge oil, wet hemp line, frying shallots from the shelter galley down the passageway, and the sharp, vinegar tang of lead-acid cells venting under load.

Fifteen upturned cable spools had been arranged in a tight, inward-facing circle on the bare deckplates—strict odd parity, as the charter demanded. 

No dais. No microphone. Only the dull thrum of the tidal turbines vibrating through the hull, keeping the low-slung work lamps burning with a steady, yellow pulse.

The fifteen seated there were not politicians. They were the human residue of three collapsed regional shipping lines: a boiler-room wiper with chemical burns across his collar; a crane rigger whose spine was permanently curved from forty years of sling work; a cook from an arrested inter-island tramp; three young line-handlers from the Batam wet-docks; two river pilots whose small craft had been seized for unpaid canal dues. They sat with their forearms resting on their knees, shoulders hunched, watching the brass drum in the center of the circle.

Tan stepped forward. He did not deliver a speech. He reached into his pocket, pulled out an iron key, and unlatched the drum’s hinged inspection plate. Inside lay ninety-seven identical wooden tokens turned from mangrove heartwood, each stamped with an identification notch corresponding to a registered deckhand, engineer, or lighterman currently sheltering in the yard.

"Operational mandate for shipping dispatch," Tan announced, his voice carrying clearly without amplification over the rhythmic slosh of the tide against the outer plates. "The dispatch leader holds sole tactical authority over the southern passage until dawn. Simple majority confirms. If rejected, the drum turns again."

Tan gave the brass crank three full revolutions. The wooden tokens clattered inside like dry seed pods.

He reached in without looking. His calloused fingers emerged holding a single mangrove disc. He squinted at the notched edge, then read the registry number stamped into the grain.

"Eighty-four," Tan said. "Kasim."

A sudden, sharp rustle ran through the circle. Heads turned toward the back row of spools.

A young deckhand sitting near the shadow of a web frame froze, a half-rolled clove cigarette pinched between his fingers. 

Kasim was twenty-eight, though the harsh equatorial sun had already etched deep, crow-footed creases around his pale hazel eyes. He was missing the lower half of his left earlobe—torn away six years ago when a synthetic mooring line had parted under tension on a Singapore bunker barge—and his left ear remained half-deaf from the sonic crack of the snap-back. His hands, resting flat against his grease-stained work trousers, were broad and square, the fingernails permanently rimmed with black zinc compound that resisted every brand of pumice soap.

"Me?" Kasim’s voice was dry, cracking slightly on the vowel. He looked around the circle as if expecting someone to point out an obvious clerical error. "Uncle, I’m a deck hand. I grease fairleads and haul wire. I don’t draft passage plans."

"You know the south spit?" Jin Wei asked from the perimeter of the circle, his voice stripped of rank, flat and testing.

"I know it," Kasim muttered, his thumb tracing the frayed cuff of his sleeve. "Ran mud-scows through the mangrove channels during the sand embargo. But that’s manual steering. You’re talking about leading four loaded barges through an automated radar gate."

Across the circle, an older man with the clipped, graying mustache of a former deep-sea second mate leaned forward, his face hardening. "This is madness. Kasim doesn't know the optical mesh protocols. If the port marshal’s patrol launches close within three cables, they’ll run an active vector scan. A deckhand will panic and heave-to. We need an officer who understands admiralty arrest procedure."

"An officer with a certified ticket is a beacon on their scanners," Lin Zhang cut in from the shadow of the ladder, her voice sharp, cutting through the rising murmur. "The moment your signature hits the navigation network, their automated receivers execute the lien. Kasim has no ticket. To their surveillance algorithms, he is invisible—just another piece of ballast shifting in the hold."

"It isn't about paperwork," Kasim said suddenly.

The circle went quiet. Kasim had not stood up, but his posture had changed. The diffidence was gone, replaced by the hard, defensive economy of a man who had survived three sinkings in five years.

"The patrol launches don't watch the bottom," Kasim said, staring directly at the skeptical former mate. "They run on deep-draft bathymetry models sold by the Singapore hydrographic office. Those charts were surveyed four years ago. After the monsoon floods last November, the mud bank behind Pulau Semakau shifted two hundred meters north. If you follow an admiralty passage plan at half-ebb, your tug’s skeg hits the clay and stays there until the tide comes back. You want to run the rice barges tonight? You don't use the channel. You run them five yards off the mangrove roots, through the oyster beds, where the water’s three feet shallower than their patrol craft can draft."

He looked at his own scarred palms, then looked up at Tan.

"I can take them through," Kasim said softly. "But I don't use their harbor radio. I steer by the light of the kerosene torches on the fish stakes. If one of their tactical skiffs tries to box us in, I won't reverse engines. I'll put the barge into the soft mud and let their own wash swamp them."

Tan nodded once, then raised his right hand. "The lot has spoken. Confirm or return to the drum."

The silence in the hold lasted four heartbeats. 

Then the crane rigger raised his thick, calloused palm. The wiper followed. The young line-handlers raised theirs without hesitation. Even the graying second mate, after a bitter, swallowing pause, lifted his hand into the dim light.

Twelve of fifteen. Qualified operational majority.

Tan picked up the mangrove token, dipped it into an open tin of red lead paint, and pressed it firmly onto the wooden dispatch board hanging from the ferry’s center stanchion. The scarlet ring gleamed wetly against the gray grain.

"The passage is yours, Kasim," Tan said. "Take the barges."

Kasim swallowed, stood up, and took the laminated channel chart Lin held out to him. His hands were steady now, entirely free of the tremor that had shaken him five minutes earlier.

Before he could reach the ladder, the high gantry optical relay above the drydock gave a sharp, mechanical groan.

The blue line-of-sight laser overhead didn't just flicker—it sheared completely off, its cyan glow snapping into darkness. From the outer pier, a young rigger dropped through the hatchway three steps at a time, his bare feet slapping wet against the steel treads.

"Kasim! Captain!" the boy gasped, clutching the hatch coaming to keep from falling. "The tactical skiffs didn't circle back to the anchorage! They’ve hooked a towline to an abandoned container hull outside the breakwater—they're pulling it across the channel mouth to choke the reef!"

Kasim didn't look back at Jin Wei. He rolled his chart into a tight cylinder, stepped past the boy, and threw open the weather door into the pelting monsoon rain.

label: Chapter 21
title: Emergency medical supply run through the mangrove creeks avoids satellite infrared sensors
content:
The squall took the shipyard broadside. Rain hit the galvanized roof of Berth 8 with the dull roar of gravel tipped into an empty hopper, washing away the grease-sheen on the staging planks in foaming gray ribbons. 

Kasim didn’t use the gangway. He vaulted the low gunwale of the shallow-draft work skiff, his bare feet slapping the ridged aluminum decking. Behind him came Lin, both arms clamped across a battered, foam-lined cooler of pediatric antivenom and refrigeration-dependent cephalosporins. Her knuckles were bloodless from the grip, her wet spectacles sliding down the bridge of her nose.

"Don't set it on the bare deck," Aisyah hissed from the stern, not looking up. She was already on her knees in bilge water, hauling soaked lengths of jute burlap out of a brine bucket. "The battery hull conducts. If the casing warms those vials by two degrees, the whole batch curdles before dawn."

Kasim caught the cooler by its nylon webbing, wedging it onto two split rubber tires lashed amidships. "Tide’s dropping four inches every ten minutes," he said, his voice flat, stripped of everything but the rhythm of the water. "If the Apex skiffs have jammed the container across the main gut, they think they've bottled the basin. They aren't looking at the stilt-creeks behind the fish traps."

"Not with binoculars, they aren't," Aisyah muttered. Her fingers, raw and peeling at the tips from old electrical flash burns, worked furiously around the rectangular battery bank nestled beneath the thwart. She was lashing blocks of dry, porous clay and wet swamp silt directly to the aluminum heat sinks. "Aegis-Omni’s thermal bird clears the horizon in nine minutes. If that pack radiates more than twenty degrees above the water temperature, we’ll show up on their terminal like a flare in an alley."

Lin dropped onto the thwart beside the cooler, her breathing shallow, rattled by the migraine behind her temples. The air smelled of rotting mangrove tannins, ozone, and the sour chemical bite of heated insulation. "Can we run dead silent?"

"No such thing as dead silent in three feet of water," Kasim said. 

He cast off the bowline. The current caught the blunt nose immediately, slewing them out from beneath the shelter of the crane tracks into the churning black gut of the channel. 

The mainland lights were already dying behind them, swallowed by the monsoon squall. Ahead lay the eastern lip of Pulau Semakau: a wall of tangled nipa palms and stilt-rooted red mangroves that looked, in the darkness, like an unbroken palisade of iron rebar. 

Kasim took the tiller of the low-profile electric drive. He didn't engage the throttle to its stop. He nudged it forward until the propeller blades gave a low, dull hum through the bottom plating—a sound felt in the shins rather than heard. The skiff surged forward, hugging the shelving mudbank where the deeper patrol hulls dared not venture.

To their left, four cables out in the open shipping fairway, the scuttled container ship lay wedged at an angle across the reef channel. Even through the sheets of downpour, the red and green running lights of two Apex tactical skiffs were visible, idling against the rusted hull plates like predatory water beetles, their twin outboards muttering in low, rhythmic growls. They were waiting for anyone attempting to run the deep-water gate.

"Five minutes to overhead transit," Lin whispered, checking the mechanical pocket chronometer tied to her wrist with sailing twine. Her fingers twitched against her oilskin coat, a nervous tic left over from months in windowless logistics basements where the hum of cooling fans had measured out the hours of her life. "Once the sweep starts, it lasts three hundred seconds. If we're under the canopy by then, the foliage scatters the signature."

"If the prop doesn't bind," Aisyah said. She had her palm flat against the motor housing, monitoring its temperature by touch. The skin of her forearm was covered in goosebumps, shivering against the tepid rain. "The silt’s thick here. The cooling intake is drawing mud."

"Then blow it clear with the hand pump," Kasim replied without turning his head. 

His eyes were locked on a faint, irregular break in the tree line—a notch where the brackish runoff of the high interior creeks cut a passage through the roots. As a boy, before the petrochemical berths had swallowed the coastline in corrugated steel and high-pressure bunkering pipes, he had set wire crab pots in these cuts with his uncle. Back then, the old man had warned him that the mud had an appetite: lose your way on a falling tide, and the swamp would suck the shoes off your feet and leave your boat perched high on stilt-roots like a crow’s nest.

The skiff slipped beneath the overhanging boughs. 

Instantly, the roar of the squall softened, transformed into a continuous, heavy patter against the thick canopy of leaves. The temperature jumped three degrees; the air turned stagnant, thick with the sulfurous stench of anaerobic silt and decaying sea-grapes. The branches scraped against the aluminum gunwales with the screech of fingernails on chalkboard.

"Cut the power," Kasim commanded softly.

Aisyah pulled the mechanical disconnect pin. The hum of the motor died. The skiff slid forward on its own momentum, the hull brushing past thick, gnarled roots that dipped into the black water like spiders' legs.

"Satellite’s rising," Lin said. Her voice was barely a breath. "Bearing north-northwest. It’s sweeping the sector now."

Kasim leaned forward, reaching out with a bamboo setting pole he had pulled from the bilge. He braced the tip against the root of an old mangrove apple, checking their drift. The current here was counter-intuitive, split by the rising mud shoals into a dozen conflicting eddies that wanted to twist the skiff sideways and jam it broadside between two trunks.

Above them, through the gaps in the dripping leaves, the sky was a bruised, slate-colored purple. They couldn't see the satellite—hundreds of miles up in the cold vacuum, its cryogenic lenses mapping every heat differential on the strait's surface down to a fraction of an inch—but they felt it like an invisible weight pressing on the back of their necks. 

Every hot wire, every friction point on the propeller shaft, every lungful of thirty-seven-degree air Lin exhaled was a beacon waiting to be indexed by an algorithmic queue in a temperature-controlled server vault in Jurong.

"Motor housing is spiking," Aisyah whispered. Panic tightened the edges of her words. She was feeling the aluminum fins beneath the burlap. "The mud jammed the cooling channel before we killed it. The heat sink is bleeding into the mount."

"Burlap," Kasim said, his teeth clenched as he fought the pole against the suction of the clay bed. "Douse it."

Lin didn't hesitate. She plunged both hands into the dark, foul water over the side, scooping up handfuls of cold river-bottom sludge, slapping it directly onto the top of the casing. The stench was sickening—ancient rot and iron rust—but the wet muck hissed softly, swallowing the escaping heat before it could bloom upward into the gap between the branches.

For forty seconds, no one moved. The only sound was the dripping of rain from Lin's chin onto the lid of the cooler, and the thick, wet sucking sound of the tide draining beneath their keel.

The hull gave a sudden, grinding shudder.

Kasim froze, his weight pressed into the pole. The skiff had stopped. 

"We’re aground," Aisyah breathed.

"Not aground," Kasim said. He looked down over the low side. In the gloom, the dark form of a submerged tree trunk—a fallen nipah palm, long drowned and calcified by barnacles—lay wedged across the channel, six inches below the surface. The aluminum bow had ridden straight onto it, the weight of the battery pack pinning them down.

Lin checked the dial on her wrist. "Two minutes left in the transit window. If we thrash, the thermal sensors catch the water disturbance."

"We don't thrash," Kasim said. He laid the pole quietly across the thwarts. "We get out."

Without waiting for an answer, he swung his legs over the side. He sank instantly to his thighs in the thick, viscous mud, the cold muck filling his canvas trousers like lead shot. His feet slid on the slimy curve of the sunken log, searching for purchase among razor-sharp clusters of oyster shells. 

Aisyah followed him on the starboard side, slipping into the black water with a sharp intake of breath as the shells tore through the knee of her work trousers. 

Together, their shoulders braced against the aluminum bow plates, they pushed. 

The mud fought them with terrifying mechanical leverage. It wasn't just friction; it was a vacuum, holding the flat bottom of the skiff like a rubber suction cup. Kasim’s breath tore through his nostrils in ragged, muffled gasps. His bad shoulder—stiffened by years of deck-winch strain—burned as if someone were driving a hot awl through the socket. 

Beside him, Aisyah’s face was twisted in the dark, her neck cords standing out, her scarred fingers slipping against the wet metal.

"On three," Kasim hissed. "Lift. Don't push. Lift the nose."

Lin shifted her weight toward the stern, pulling the cooler against her belly to counter the balance, her eyes wide behind her rain-streaked lenses.

"One," Kasim grunted. "Two... heave."

They threw their spines into it. The bow rose an inch, two inches. The bottom scraped over the barnacled wood with a sound like tearing tin. The suction broke with a wet, hollow *thwip*, and the skiff shot forward into the deeper pool beyond the log.

Aisyah scrambled back over the gunwale, coughing up brackish water she had swallowed when her footing slipped. Kasim dragged himself up after her, his shins bleeding freely from shallow oyster cuts that stung with the sharp bite of sea salt.

Lin let out a long, trembling exhalation, tapping the crystal of her watch. "Window closed. The bird is over the Malacca approaches."

Kasim lay on the deck boards for three heartbeats, letting the cold rain wash the mud from his face. Then he sat up, wiping his eyes with the back of a bloody wrist.

"Aisyah. Clear the intake."

She nodded, her teeth chattering so hard she couldn't speak, and reached for the wire clearing rod under the seat.

Before her hand touched the tool, the darkness shattered.

Fifty yards behind them, back where the creek mouth opened into the bay, an engine revved—not the muffled growl of their electric drive, but the sharp, metallic scream of a twin-rotor interceptor skiff throttling up to plan speed. A blue halogen beam tore through the mangrove canopy, slicing between the gnarled branches like a broadsword, illuminating the rising steam of their own breath against the black leaves.

The patrol boat hadn't used the satellite. 

It was drifting on a passive acoustic hydrophone, listening for the scrape of aluminum against drowned wood—and it had just found it.

label: Chapter 22
title: Lin presents the UNCLOS Immaterial Commons Brief, converting the hub into an internationally protected refuge
content:
The halogen blade sheared through the black leaves overhead, turning the drizzle into a curtain of falling needles.

"Down," Kasim rasped.

He didn't reach for a throttle. An engine rev would give their vector away to the hydrophone before the propeller could bite water. Instead, he shoved his calloused palm against the muddy bank, guiding the skiff’s nose deeper into the tangle of stilt roots. The sharp, vinegary smell of disturbed mangrove peat rose around them, thick enough to choke on.

Behind them, the twin-rotor interceptor surged into the creek mouth, its heavy hull pushing a bow wave that sloshed violently against the mudflats. The wash rocked the small aluminum skiff, lifting it inches, then dropping it into the silt with a sickening suck.

Aisyah worked on her knees in the bilge, her knuckles bloody from the oyster beds, sliding the wire clearing rod into the waterjet intake. Her fingers, burned raw years ago by switchboard flashovers, lacked sensation at the tips; she had to feel the jammed mangrove twigs through the vibration in her wrists. She twisted the steel wire once, twice, until a knot of fibrous root broke free with a wet pop.

"Clear," she whispered, her voice barely carrying past her cracked lips.

The searchlight swept twenty paces to their port side, incinerating the dark. It pinned a cluster of drowning pneumatophores in stark, blinding silver. A voice boomed over a marine hailer—flat, compressed, stripped of humanity by algorithmic amplification: *Vessel in unchartered shallows, cut your drives and prepare to be boarded under Admiralty salvage writ.*

Kasim didn't move. A drop of blood crawled from his temple, tracking through the river mud crusted along his jawline. He reached into his coat and produced an unlit cigarette—stale, bent nearly in half from three days crushed behind his compass case—and placed the dry paper between his lips, chewing on the bitter tobacco without lighting it. It was an old habit from his early days on the night tugs, something to keep his jaw from clenching until his molars cracked.

"They're drawing five feet," Kasim breathed into Lin’s ear. "We draw six inches. Hold the rail."

He dipped a single wooden sculling oar over the stern, feathering the blade so quietly that the dark water parted without a gurgle. He didn't fight the interceptor’s wake; he rode it. As the backwash bounced off the mangrove shelf, it carried them sideways through an archway of drowned roots into the deep dredged drainage flume of Drydock 4.

The searchlight wheeled away, scouring the empty mudbank where they had grounded three minutes before.

Ten minutes later, the aluminum hull bumped against the slime-slick timber fenders of Berth 9. 

The Keppel-Batam yard smelled of wet iron, diesel residue, and the sweet, decaying ozone of the massive battery banks working under load. Rain drummed on the corrugated iron overhangs sixty feet above. Uncle Tan stood waiting on the pontoon, his woolen watch-cap pulled down over ears swollen with gout. He didn't ask questions.
